 * ├── rust-toolchain.toml
 * ├── .cargo/config.toml
 * ├── .gitignore
 * ├── crates/native/    cdylib binding
 * └── npm/native/       @scope/native — platform packages are generated in CI
 * ```
 *
 * Supports any number of crates: add one with `m native add <name>` (or
 * `m native add shared --pure` for a crate with no Node-API surface). Cargo runs
 * against the whole workspace; napi runs per package.
 *
 * Registered as the `native` feature's setup step in the registry (`FEATURES`).
 */

const TARGET_DIR = process.cwd();
/** Rewritten by the scaffolder (and by CI/local git) — never a real repo. */
const REPO_PLACEHOLDER = "Archont561/ts-monorepo-template";
const NATIVE_ROOT = join(TARGET_DIR, NATIVE_DIR);
const REPO_URL = repositoryUrl();
/** Rewritten by the scaffolder — the npm scope every generated manifest uses. */
const SCOPE = process.env.NATIVE_SCOPE ?? DEFAULT_NATIVE_SCOPE;

const ROOT_PACKAGE_JSON = join(TARGET_DIR, "package.json");
const TURBO_BASE = join(TARGET_DIR, CONFIGS_RELATIVE, "turbo.base.json");
const EXAMPLE_NATIVE_DIR = join(TARGET_DIR, "apps/example/src/pages/api/native");

const WORKSPACE_MANIFEST = join(NATIVE_ROOT, "Cargo.toml");
const TOOLCHAIN = join(NATIVE_ROOT, "rust-toolchain.toml");
const ROOT_TOOLCHAIN = join(TARGET_DIR, "rust-toolchain.toml");
const CARGO_CONFIG = join(NATIVE_ROOT, ".cargo/config.toml");
const ROOT_CARGO_CONFIG = join(TARGET_DIR, ".cargo/config.toml");
const NATIVE_GITIGNORE = join(NATIVE_ROOT, ".gitignore");

/** Root scripts the workspace needs, and the m native command each one runs. */
const ROOT_SCRIPTS: Record<string, string> = {
  "build:native": "m native napi:build",
  "build:wasm": "m native napi:build:wasm",
  "test:native": "m native test",
};

/** Turbo tasks for the native builds — cargo stays uncached. */
/**
 * The two tasks as JSON text in the style of `turbo.base.json` — short arrays
 * stay inline there, which is exactly what a re-serialized object would lose.
 */
const TURBO_TASKS: Record<string, string> = {
  "build:native": `{
  "dependsOn": ["^build"],
  "outputs": ["*.node", "index.js", "index.d.ts"],
  "cache": false
}`,
  "build:wasm": `{
  "dependsOn": ["build:native"],
  "outputs": ["*.wasi.cjs", "*.wasi-browser.js", "*.wasm"],
  "cache": false
}`,
};

/** The example routes, written verbatim — they talk to @scope/native via external. */
const EXAMPLE_ROUTES: Record<string, string> = {
  "index.ts": `// TEMPLATE-ONLY:START(native)
export default function handleNativeIndex(): Response {
  return Response.json({
    message: "Native bindings (Rust via napi-rs) with JS fallback",
    endpoints: [
      "/api/native/add?a=1&b=2",
      "/api/native/fibonacci/:n",
      "/api/native/primes/:n",
      "/api/native/reverse?text=hello",
      "/api/native/status",
    ],
  });
}
// TEMPLATE-ONLY:END(native)
`,
  "add.ts": `// TEMPLATE-ONLY:START(native)
import { addFallback, addSync, isNativeAvailable } from "@myorg/external";
export default async function handleNativeAdd(req: Request): Promise<Response> {
  const url = new URL(req.url);
  const a = Number(url.searchParams.get("a") ?? "1");
  const b = Number(url.searchParams.get("b") ?? "2");
  const result = addSync(a, b);
  return Response.json({ a, b, result, fallback: addFallback(a,b), native: isNativeAvailable() ? "rust" : "js-fallback" });
}
// TEMPLATE-ONLY:END(native)
`,
  "status.ts": `// TEMPLATE-ONLY:START(native)
import { isNativeAvailable } from "@myorg/external";
export default async function handleNativeStatus(): Promise<Response> {
  let nativeBinding: unknown = null;
  try {
    // @ts-expect-error optional
    const mod = await import("@myorg/native");
    nativeBinding = Object.keys(mod);
  } catch {}
  return Response.json({ isNativeAvailable: isNativeAvailable(), nativeBinding });
}
// TEMPLATE-ONLY:END(native)
`,
};

async function exists(path: string): Promise<boolean> {
  return (await file(path).exists()) || (await $`test -d ${path}`.nothrow().quiet()).exitCode === 0;
}

/**
 * Repository URL for the generated manifests.
 *
 * Prefers the repo Actions is running in, then the local git remote, so a
 * project never inherits the template's URL. Falls back to an obvious
 * placeholder the scaffolder rewrites.
 */
function repositoryUrl(): string {
  const fromEnv = process.env.GITHUB_REPOSITORY;
  if (fromEnv) return `https://github.com/${fromEnv}`;

  const remote = spawnSync(["git", "config", "--get", "remote.origin.url"], { stdout: "pipe" })
    .stdout?.toString()
    .trim();
  if (remote) {
    const match = remote.match(/github\.com[:/]([^/]+)\/(.+?)(\.git)?$/);
    if (match) return `https://github.com/${match[1]}/${match[2]}`;
  }

  return `https://github.com/${REPO_PLACEHOLDER}`;
}

/** Relative-to-root logging, so the output never leaks absolute temp paths. */
function relative(path: string): string {
  return path.replace(`${TARGET_DIR}/`, "");
}

/**
 * Moves a pre-workspace `packages/native/{src,build.rs,Cargo.toml}` package
 * into `crates/<name>/` so older projects pick up the new shape on setup.
 */
async function migrateLegacyCrate(name: string): Promise<boolean> {
  if (!(await file(WORKSPACE_MANIFEST).exists())) return false;
  const content = await file(WORKSPACE_MANIFEST).text();
  if (!content.includes("[package]")) return false;

  const crateDir = join(TARGET_DIR, nativeCrateDir(name));
  if (await exists(crateDir)) return false;

  console.log(`  📦 Migrating the single-crate layout into crates/${name}/...`);
  await mkdir(join(crateDir, "src"), { recursive: true });
  await $`cp -r ${join(NATIVE_ROOT, "src")} ${join(crateDir, "src")} 2>/dev/null`.nothrow().quiet();
  if (await file(join(NATIVE_ROOT, "build.rs")).exists()) {
    await $`mv ${join(NATIVE_ROOT, "build.rs")} ${join(crateDir, "build.rs")}`.quiet();
  }
  await $`rm -rf ${join(NATIVE_ROOT, "src")}`.quiet();
  await $`rm -f ${WORKSPACE_MANIFEST}`.quiet();

  // The npm package used to live at the workspace root — move it under npm/.
  const legacyPackage = join(NATIVE_ROOT, "package.json");
  const packageDir = join(TARGET_DIR, nativePackageDir(name));
  if ((await file(legacyPackage).exists()) && !(await file(packageDir).exists())) {
    await mkdir(packageDir, { recursive: true });
    await $`mv ${legacyPackage} ${join(packageDir, "package.json")}`.quiet();
    for (const extra of ["tsconfig.json", "turbo.json", "README.md"]) {
      if (await file(join(NATIVE_ROOT, extra)).exists()) {
        await $`mv ${join(NATIVE_ROOT, extra)} ${join(packageDir, extra)}`.quiet();
      }
    }
    if (await exists(join(NATIVE_ROOT, "tests"))) {
      await mkdir(join(packageDir, "tests"), { recursive: true });
      await $`sh -c 'mv ${join(NATIVE_ROOT, "tests")}/* ${join(packageDir, "tests")}/ 2>/dev/null'`
        .nothrow()
        .quiet();
      await $`rm -rf ${join(NATIVE_ROOT, "tests")}`.quiet();
    }
  }
  console.log(`  ✓ Moved crate + npm package under packages/native/`);
  return true;
}

/** Brings a project that predates the Cargo workspace onto the current layout. */
async function migrateLegacyLayout(): Promise<void> {
  for (const spec of DEFAULT_NATIVE_CRATES) {
    await migrateLegacyCrate(spec.name);
  }
}

/** Writes the crates + npm packages that are missing, leaving existing ones alone. */
async function writeCrates(): Promise<NativeCrateSpec[]> {
  const crates: NativeCrateSpec[] = [];
  for (const spec of DEFAULT_NATIVE_CRATES) {
    const crateDir = join(TARGET_DIR, nativeCrateDir(spec.name));
    if (await exists(join(crateDir, "Cargo.toml"))) {
      console.log(`  ✓ ${nativeCrateDir(spec.name)}/ exists`);
    } else {
      const written = await writeCrate(TARGET_DIR, spec, { scope: SCOPE, repository: REPO_URL });
      console.log(
        `  ✓ ${relative(written.crate)}/ (crate)${written.package ? ` + ${relative(written.package)}/ (npm)` : ""}`,
      );
    }
    crates.push(spec);
  }
  return crates;
}

/**
 * Bridge node — the single Turbo package for every pure Rust crate. Refreshed
 * from the templates on every setup so it can never drift.
 */
async function syncBridgeNode(): Promise<void> {
  await writeBridgeNode(TARGET_DIR, { scope: SCOPE, repository: REPO_URL });
  console.log("  ✓ packages/native/crates/ (pure-Rust bridge node)");
}

/** Virtual workspace manifest — members are re-synced, never clobbered. */
async function syncWorkspaceManifest(crates: NativeCrateSpec[]): Promise<void> {
  if (await file(WORKSPACE_MANIFEST).exists()) {
    for (const spec of crates) await addWorkspaceMember(TARGET_DIR, spec.name);
    console.log("  ✓ packages/native/Cargo.toml (members synced)");
    return;
  }

  await writeFile(
    WORKSPACE_MANIFEST,
    workspaceCargoToml(crates, { scope: SCOPE, repository: REPO_URL }),
  );
  console.log("  ✓ packages/native/Cargo.toml (virtual workspace, resolver 3)");
}

/** Toolchain pin: adopt one left at the repo root, otherwise write the default. */
async function setupToolchain(): Promise<void> {
  if (await file(TOOLCHAIN).exists()) return;

  if (await file(ROOT_TOOLCHAIN).exists()) {
    await writeFile(TOOLCHAIN, await file(ROOT_TOOLCHAIN).text());
    await $`rm -f ${ROOT_TOOLCHAIN}`.quiet();
    console.log("  ✓ Moved rust-toolchain.toml into packages/native/");
    return;
  }

  await writeFile(TOOLCHAIN, rustToolchainToml());
  console.log("  ✓ packages/native/rust-toolchain.toml (stable + wasm32-wasip1-threads)");
}

/** Cargo config lives with the crates — a root-level one is migrated and removed. */
async function setupCargoConfig(): Promise<void> {
  if (!(await file(CARGO_CONFIG).exists())) {
    await mkdir(join(NATIVE_ROOT, ".cargo"), { recursive: true });
    await writeFile(
      CARGO_CONFIG,
      (await file(ROOT_CARGO_CONFIG).exists())
        ? await file(ROOT_CARGO_CONFIG).text()
        : cargoConfigToml(),
    );
    console.log("  ✓ packages/native/.cargo/config.toml");
  }

  if (!(await file(ROOT_CARGO_CONFIG).exists())) return;

  await $`rm -f ${ROOT_CARGO_CONFIG}`.quiet();
  await $`rmdir ${join(TARGET_DIR, ".cargo")}`.nothrow().quiet();
}

async function ensureNativeGitignore(): Promise<void> {
  if (await file(NATIVE_GITIGNORE).exists()) return;

  await writeFile(NATIVE_GITIGNORE, nativeGitignore());
  console.log("  ✓ packages/native/.gitignore (target/, generated loaders, npm/*-*/)");
}

interface RootManifest {
  scripts?: Record<string, string>;
  workspaces?: string[];
}

/** Root package.json — link the npm packages into the Bun workspace. */
async function linkNpmPackages(): Promise<void> {
  await updateManifestFile(ROOT_PACKAGE_JSON, (source) => {
    const pkg = readJson<RootManifest>(source);
    let next = source;

    if (!(pkg.workspaces ?? []).includes(NATIVE_WORKSPACE_GLOB)) {
      console.log(`  ✓ Added workspace glob ${NATIVE_WORKSPACE_GLOB}`);
      next = addJsonArrayValue(next, "workspaces", NATIVE_WORKSPACE_GLOB);
    }

    // The bridge node is a single package (not a glob) so the crates dir
    // itself is never treated as a workspace member.
    const bridgeEntry = `${NATIVE_DIR}/crates`;
    if (!(pkg.workspaces ?? []).includes(bridgeEntry)) {
      console.log(`  ✓ Added workspace entry ${bridgeEntry} (pure-Rust bridge node)`);
      next = addJsonArrayValue(next, "workspaces", bridgeEntry);
    }

    for (const [name, command] of Object.entries(ROOT_SCRIPTS)) {
      if (pkg.scripts?.[name] === command) continue;
      console.log(`  ✓ Set root script ${name} → ${command}`);
      next = setJsonValue(next, `scripts.${name}`, command);
    }

    for (const name of Object.keys(pkg.scripts ?? {})) {
      const command = pkg.scripts?.[name] ?? "";
      if (!name.startsWith("cargo:") || !command.includes("bun --filter")) continue;
      console.log(`  🗑️ Removed root script ${name} (cargo goes through m native)`);
      next = removeJsonEntry(next, `scripts.${name}`);
    }

    return next;
  });
}

/** Turbo tasks — one build per npm package, cargo stays uncached. */
async function ensureTurboTasks(): Promise<void> {
  await updateManifestFile(TURBO_BASE, (source) => {
    const turbo = readJson<{ tasks?: Record<string, unknown> }>(source);
    let next = source;

    for (const [name, task] of Object.entries(TURBO_TASKS)) {
      if (turbo.tasks?.[name]) continue;
      console.log(`  ✓ Added turbo task ${name}`);
      next = setJsonBlock(next, `tasks.${name}`, task);
    }

    return next;
  });
}

/** Example routes — unchanged, they talk to @scope/native through external. */
async function writeExampleRoutes(): Promise<void> {
  if (await exists(EXAMPLE_NATIVE_DIR)) return;

  console.log("  📦 Creating example native routes...");
  // The per-endpoint folders exist for future pages; the routes themselves sit
  // flat in the folder above them.
  await mkdir(join(EXAMPLE_NATIVE_DIR, "fibonacci"), { recursive: true });
  await mkdir(join(EXAMPLE_NATIVE_DIR, "primes"), { recursive: true });

  for (const [name, contents] of Object.entries(EXAMPLE_ROUTES)) {
    await writeFile(join(EXAMPLE_NATIVE_DIR, name), contents);
  }
  console.log("  ✓ Example native routes");
}

function printNextSteps(): void {
  console.log("\n✅ Native setup complete (Cargo workspace + napi-rs).\n");
  console.log("  Layout:");
  console.log(`    ${NATIVE_DIR}/Cargo.toml       virtual workspace`);
  console.log(`    ${NATIVE_DIR}/crates/<name>/   one crate per Rust unit`);
  console.log(`    ${NATIVE_DIR}/npm/<name>/      one npm package per binding\n`);
  console.log("  Commands:");
  console.log("    m native list              # crates + packages");
  console.log("    m native add <name>        # add a crate (+ npm package)");
  console.log("    m native add shared --pure # pure Rust crate, no Node-API");
  console.log("    m native check             # cargo check --workspace");
  console.log("    m native napi:build        # build every package's .node");
  console.log("    m native napi:build:wasm   # wasm32-wasip1-threads\n");
  console.log("  Next: bun install && m native check && bun run build:native\n");
}

async function main() {
  console.log("\n🦀 Setting up native Rust bindings (Cargo workspace + napi-rs)...\n");
  console.log(`  Mode: Cargo workspace at ${NATIVE_DIR}/ (crates/* + npm/*)`);
  console.log("  CLI: m native (cargo + napi wrapper)\n");

  await mkdir(NATIVE_ROOT, { recursive: true });

  await migrateLegacyLayout();
  const crates = await writeCrates();
  await syncWorkspaceManifest(crates);
  await syncBridgeNode();
  await setupToolchain();
  await setupCargoConfig();
  await ensureNativeGitignore();
  await linkNpmPackages();
  await ensureTurboTasks();
  await writeExampleRoutes();
  printNextSteps();
}

if (import.meta.main) {
  await main();
}

      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # The napi-rs images are Debian-based but ship neither `unzip` nor a musl
      # libc toolchain, and both are needed before anything else can run:
      #   * `oven-sh/setup-bun` downloads Bun as a .zip and extracts it by
      #     shelling out to `unzip` — without it the step dies with "Unable to
      #     locate executable file: unzip" before a single crate is compiled.
      #   * the musl target needs `musl-gcc`; napi runs a plain
      #     `cargo build --target <triple>`, so cargo takes the linker from the
      #     standard CARGO_TARGET_*_LINKER variable set just below.
      # Runs before setup-bun on purpose — it is the step that needs unzip.
      - name: Install container prerequisites
        if: matrix.container != ''
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          apt-get update
          apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends unzip ca-certificates musl-tools
        shell: bash

      - uses: oven-sh/setup-bun@v2
        with:
          bun-version: {{BUN_VERSION}}

      - name: Setup Rust toolchain
        uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          targets: ${{ matrix.target }}

      - name: Rust cache
        uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
        with:
          workspaces: "{{NATIVE_DIR}}"
          key: ${{ matrix.target }}

      # `rust-toolchain.toml` pins the channel only, so a non-host target has to
      # be added by the job that builds it — the step above does that. musl
      # additionally needs its linker named, because the host linker produces
      # glibc binaries.
      - name: Use musl-gcc as the linker
        if: matrix.target == 'x86_64-unknown-linux-musl'
        run: echo "CARGO_TARGET_X86_64_UNKNOWN_LINUX_MUSL_LINKER=musl-gcc" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
        shell: bash

      # The WASI SDK provides the clang that links wasm32-wasip1-threads.
      - name: Install WASI SDK
        if: matrix.wasi
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          curl -fsSL -o wasi-sdk.tar.gz \
            "https://github.com/WebAssembly/wasi-sdk/releases/download/wasi-sdk-${WASI_SDK_VERSION}/wasi-sdk-${WASI_SDK_VERSION}.0-x86_64-linux.tar.gz"
          mkdir -p "${RUNNER_TEMP}/wasi-sdk"
          tar -xzf wasi-sdk.tar.gz -C "${RUNNER_TEMP}/wasi-sdk" --strip-components=1
          echo "WASI_SDK_PATH=${RUNNER_TEMP}/wasi-sdk" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
        shell: bash

      - run: bun install --frozen-lockfile

      # One triple per job — `napi build` cannot cross-compile them all at once.
      - name: Build bindings
        run: bunx m native napi:build --target ${{ matrix.target }}
        shell: bash

      - name: Upload bindings
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v6
        with:
          name: bindings-${{ matrix.target }}
          path: |
            {{NATIVE_DIR}}/npm/*/*.node
            {{NATIVE_DIR}}/npm/*/*.wasm
            {{NATIVE_DIR}}/npm/*/*.mjs
            {{NATIVE_DIR}}/npm/*/*.cjs
          if-no-files-found: error

import { APP_FILES, type FeatureFiles } from "./paths";
import type { FeatureProvider } from "./provider";

/** Endpoints the native routes expose — mirrors what `/api/native` reports. */
export const NATIVE_ENDPOINTS = [
  "/api/native",
  "/api/native/add?a=1&b=2",
  "/api/native/fibonacci/:n",
  "/api/native/primes/:n",
  "/api/native/reverse?text=hello",
  "/api/native/status",
];

/** Native bindings are available while the native routes exist. */
export async function hasNative(files: FeatureFiles = APP_FILES): Promise<boolean> {
  try {
    return await files.app("src/pages/api/native/index.ts").exists();
  } catch {
    return false;
  }
}

/** Native detection and the endpoints it contributes to the API index. */
export function nativeProvider(files: FeatureFiles = APP_FILES): FeatureProvider {
  return {
    name: "native",
    enabled: () => hasNative(files),
    endpoints: () => [...NATIVE_ENDPOINTS],
  };
}

/** The provider the app uses. */
export const native: FeatureProvider = nativeProvider();

import { file } from "bun";

/**
 * App paths, resolved once.
 *
 * Every path is resolved from *this* module's location, so the app root is two
 * levels up: `public/` is `../../public` from `features/`. Spelling the relative
 * path out per call site is how the lookups drifted — `../../public/...` from
 * `src/` resolved to `apps/public/`, which does not exist, so every lookup
 * silently missed and the feature flags were always reported as off.
 */

/**
 * `apps/example/` — the app root that owns `public/` and `src/`.
 *
 * Exported so nothing else in the app has to spell a `../../` chain to reach it.
 * The `/dist/` branch matters: the built bundle sits one level shallower than
 * the source, so a single relative path is wrong in one of the two.
 */
export const APP_ROOT = new URL(
  import.meta.url.includes("/dist/") ? "../" : "../../",
  import.meta.url,
);

/** Repository root — the monorepo that owns `packages/` and `apps/`. */
export const REPO_ROOT = new URL(
  import.meta.url.includes("/dist/") ? "../../../" : "../../../../",
  import.meta.url,
);

/** A file inside the app, e.g. `appFile("public/index.html")`. */
export function appFile(path: string): ReturnType<typeof file> {
  return file(new URL(path, APP_ROOT));
}

/** A file at the repo root, e.g. `repoFile("packages/tooling/src/configs/biome.json")`. */
export function repoFile(path: string): ReturnType<typeof file> {
  return file(new URL(path, REPO_ROOT));
}

/**
 * Where a feature looks for its files.
 *
 * Injectable so a test can point a provider at a fixture directory instead of
 * this checkout — the failure mode when the real paths are wrong is silence.
 */
export interface FeatureFiles {
  /** A file inside the app. */
  app(path: string): ReturnType<typeof file>;
  /** A file at the repository root. */
  repo(path: string): ReturnType<typeof file>;
}

/** The real app: everything relative to this module. */
export const APP_FILES: FeatureFiles = { app: appFile, repo: repoFile };

  Line 17: - Generated, never committed as source: `.github/workflows/*`, `turbo.json`, `lefthook.yml`, `packages/native/npm/*-*/`

  Line 30: | `@myorg/native` | Rust bindings built from `packages/native/crates/native` (opt-in) | ✅ npm |

  Line 33: `packages/tooling` is private. `packages/native` itself is a Cargo workspace root,

  Line 34: not an npm package — the npm package is `packages/native/npm/native`.

  Line 53: - **Native is a virtual Cargo workspace** — `packages/native/crates/*` for Rust, `packages/native/npm/*` for the npm packages; per-platform packages are CI artifacts only.

  Line 61: - Branch `arena/01a0a0bf-ts-monorepo-template`. Rust integration after the Bun+Turbo+Cargo guide (rustup itself impossible in the sandbox — TLS-blocked — so the Rust layer is verified by structure tests only): `packages/native` now splits logic from bindings — new pure crate `crates/shared` (add, fibonacci, reverse_string, primes_up_to, Counter + tests; no napi), `crates/native` reduced to thin `#[napi]` wrappers via `shared.workspace = true`. Pure crates form ONE Turbo node: the bridge package `packages/native/crates/package.json` (`@myorg/native-crates`, scripts `mnative build/test --pure`), in root `workspaces`; bindings with Cargo path deps carry `@myorg/native-crates: workspace:*` so Turbo orders pure Rust before napi builds. `mnative` gained `sync` (refresh bridge + mirror/drop the `workspace:*` edges to match Cargo path deps — discover.ts now resolves both `{path = …}` and `x.workspace = true` spellings) and `--pure` on build/check/clippy/fmt/fmt:check/test. `@myorg/native#build` is now Turbo-**cached** (outputs `*.node`/`index.js`/`index.d.ts`; inputs `../../crates/*/src/**/*.rs` + crate manifests + `../../Cargo.toml|Cargo.lock|rust-toolchain.toml` — verified: touching a `.rs` changes the task hash); bridge + wasm tasks stay uncached (cargo owns `target/`). `[profile.release]` (lto, codegen-units 1, strip) and the previously missing `[profile.ci]` are now actually emitted. Scaffolder/setup/tests/docs updated; CLI-contract snapshot refreshed (sync command).

  Line 70: - Scaffolds now match the picture the docs promised: the root manifest is reconciled with what survived a removal (`bun install` no longer fails on a deleted `packages/native`), scripts whose bin was removed are gone (`security:audit`, `skills`, `security:trivy`/`security:check`), and native-only test imports are wrapped in `TEMPLATE-ONLY` markers.

  Line 80: - `bun install` links `node_modules/@myorg/native` → `packages/native/npm/native`

  Line 111: | `0834b0a` | `packages/native` becomes a virtual Cargo workspace (`crates/*` + `npm/*`) |

  Line 121: - `packages/native` has no `package.json` — it is a Cargo workspace root, and its npm package is one level deeper (`npm/native`)

  Line 122: - `packages/native/npm/native` builds with `mnative napi:build --only native`, not `mbunup`

## Target layout

```
repo root/
├── Cargo.toml           # virtual workspace root (moved from packages/native)
├── rust-toolchain.toml
├── .cargo/config.toml
├── crates/              # Rust only + the bridge node
│   ├── package.json     # @myorg/native-crates (bridge node, moved 1 level up)
│   ├── turbo.json
│   ├── native/          # binding crate
│   └── shared/          # pure crate
├── packages/
│   └── native/npm/      # @myorg/native stays EXACTLY where it is
│       └── native/      #   (so per-platform packages, workflows, gitignore, Dockerfile runtime copies stay untouched)
└── apps/
```

The `crates/*` crate dirs and the bridge node sit directly under root, side by side with `packages/` and `apps/`. Because the bridge stays one level below `Cargo.toml`, its `crates/turbo.json` relative inputs (`../Cargo.toml`, `*/src/**/*.rs`) are byte-identical after the move.

# [#](#create-npm-dirs) Create Npm Dirs

Create npm package dirs for different platforms

## [#](#when-you-need-this) When you need this

`napi create-npm-dirs` creates one `npm/<platform-arch-abi>` directory per entry of the `napi.targets` config, each containing a ready-to-publish `package.json` for that platform's package. Committing these directories is no longer recommended; create them in CI instead. You need this command before [`napi artifacts`](./artifacts) can copy built binaries into the platform packages, and before [`napi pre-publish`](./pre-publish) can publish them.

In the release pipeline this command sits after the platform `napi build` jobs and before `napi artifacts`. See [Release native packages](/docs/deep-dive/release) for the complete pipeline.

## [#](#usage) Usage

sh

```
# CLI
napi create-npm-dirs [--options]
```

typescript

```
// Programmatically
import { NapiCli } from '@napi-rs/cli'

new NapiCli().createNpmDirs({
  // options
})
```

## [#](#examples) Examples

Create the platform package directories in a CI release job:

sh

```
napi create-npm-dirs
```

Preview which directories and files would be created, without touching the file system:

sh

```
napi create-npm-dirs --dry-run
```

# [#](#artifacts) Artifacts

`napi artifacts` recursively finds built `.node` and `.wasm` files, validates their binary names and target suffixes, and copies them into the matching per-platform npm packages. Native files are also copied to the root package directory so the generated loader can resolve a local binding.

## [#](#usage) Usage

sh

```
napi artifacts [--options]
```

ts

```
import { NapiCli } from '@napi-rs/cli'

await new NapiCli().artifacts({
  outputDir: 'artifacts',
  npmDir: 'npm',
})
```

## [#](#options) Options

Option

CLI syntax

Type

Required

Default

Description

`cwd`

`--cwd`

`string`

No

`process.cwd()`

Base directory for config, package, artifact-download, npm-package, and build-output paths.

`configPath`

`--config-path,-c`

`string`

No

Standalone napi config JSON file.

`packageJsonPath`

`--package-json-path`

`string`

No

`package.json`

Root package containing the napi config.

`outputDir`

`--output-dir,-o,-d`

`string`

No

`./artifacts`

Directory recursively searched for downloaded `.node` and `.wasm` files. This corresponds to the artifact-download path, not `npm/`.

`npmDir`

`--npm-dir`

`string`

No

`npm`

Directory containing the generated per-platform packages.

`buildOutputDir`

`--build-output-dir`

`string`

No

`cwd`

Directory containing generated WASI JavaScript and worker files. Relative paths resolve from `--cwd`.

There is no `--dist` option. Use `--output-dir` for downloaded build artifacts and `--npm-dir` for platform package destinations.

## [#](#ci-workflow) CI workflow

Each build job should upload files named with the configured binary name and target ABI, for example:

text

```
cool.darwin-arm64.node
cool.linux-x64-gnu.node
cool.win32-x64-msvc.node
cool.wasm32-wasi.wasm
```

In the collection job, create the package directories, download all artifacts, then collect them:

yaml

```
- name: Create platform packages
  run: yarn napi create-npm-dirs

- name: Download all build artifacts
  uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
  with:
    path: artifacts

- name: Move artifacts into packages
  run: yarn napi artifacts --output-dir artifacts --npm-dir npm
```

`actions/download-artifact` normally creates one nested directory per uploaded artifact. The CLI searches recursively, so both of these layouts work:

text

```
artifacts/
├── bindings-aarch64-apple-darwin/
│   └── cool.darwin-arm64.node
├── bindings-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/
│   └── cool.linux-x64-gnu.node
└── bindings-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/
    └── cool.win32-x64-msvc.node
```

After collection:

text

```
.
├── cool.darwin-arm64.node
├── cool.linux-x64-gnu.node
├── cool.win32-x64-msvc.node
└── npm/
    ├── darwin-arm64/cool.darwin-arm64.node
    ├── linux-x64-gnu/cool.linux-x64-gnu.node
    └── win32-x64-msvc/cool.win32-x64-msvc.node
```

## [#](#matching-rules) Matching rules

For each discovered file, the CLI:

1.  Splits the final dot-delimited suffix from the file name, such as `linux-x64-gnu`.
2.  Requires the remaining base name to equal `napi.binaryName`. A mismatched binary name is warned about and skipped.
3.  Finds the configured target package whose directory matches that platform suffix. A file with no target package causes the command to fail, except source binaries that are intentionally combined into a configured universal binary.
4.  Writes the file into that target package and the root package directory.

WARNING

The command trusts the suffix in the file name. It does not inspect the native binary to prove its architecture, libc, minimum OS, or Node-API level. Test every artifact on the runtime it claims to support before publishing.

## [#](#wasi-artifacts) WASI artifacts

When `napi.targets` contains a WASI target, `napi artifacts` also copies the generated support files into `npm/wasm32-wasi`:

-   `<binaryName>.wasi.cjs`
-   `<binaryName>.wasi-browser.js`
-   `wasi-worker.mjs`
-   `wasi-worker-browser.mjs`

By default these files are read from `--cwd`. Pass `--build-output-dir` when the WASI build wrote them elsewhere; a relative value is resolved from `--cwd`. The downloaded `.wasm` file is still discovered under `--output-dir`.

After collecting and verifying all targets, [`napi pre-publish`](./pre-publish) versions and publishes the platform packages. `napi pre-publish` does not copy missing artifacts for you.

Short version: `native/npm/native` looks weird because your demo crate is literally named **`native`**, so the feature dir, the npm container, and the crate all say the same word. The `npm/` layer itself isn't disposable — it's napi's own convention. Details below, then "how it looks when using it."

## Why `npm/` exists (and can't just go away)

Per the napi-rs CLI docs I pulled:
- `napi create-npm-dirs` + `napi artifacts` generate one per-platform publish package per entry in `napi.targets`, and their default destination is a sibling **`npm/`** directory. The generated `index.js` loader also requires optional deps named `<packageName>-<platform>` (e.g. `@myorg/native-linux-x64-gnu`) at runtime.
- So the layout is *dictated by napi*, not by the template: **base package dir + a sibling `npm/` holding `<name>-<platform>` dirs**.

That means: whichever way you flatten, an `npm/`-named sibling for platform packages survives.

## The three real placements

| Layout | Base pkg dir | Generated platform dirs | Multi-crate? | Verdict |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Current** | `packages/native/npm/native/` | `packages/native/npm/native-<platform>/` | ✅ each crate is a subdir of `npm/` | napi-conformant; "weird" is purely the crate name |
| **"native/npm"** (your idea) | `packages/native/npm/` | `packages/native/npm/<name>-<platform>/` | ❌ *exactly one* crate can own `npm/package.json` | breaks the moment you `m native add parser`; platform dirs nest inside the published package dir |
| **Full flatten** | `packages/native/` | `packages/native/npm/<name>-<platform>/` | ⚠️ 2nd crate → `packages/<name>/` at top level (pollutes `packages/*` glob + prune list) | single-crate-fine, multi-crate-ugly |

So "can I have `native/npm`?" — technically yes **for a single binding crate**, but it's the napi equivalent of `index.html/index.html/index.html`. If the triple bothers you, the zero-structural-cost fixes are:
1. Rename the demo crate (e.g. `addon`) → `packages/native/npm/addon`, published as `@myorg/addon` — reads clean, everything else untouched.
2. Rename the JS container instead (e.g. `packages/bindings/npm/native`) so the words don't rhyme.

My recommendation stays **keep `packages/native/npm/<crate>`** — it's the only shape that's napi-correct *and* multi-crate-safe, and it's what the existing `m native add`/discover/sync machinery already assumes. Options (1)/(2) are cosmetic if you want them.

## How it looks when using it

**Repo tree after a host build** (`bun run build:native`):
```
crates/                          ← Rust, at repo root
├── package.json  turbo.json     ← @myorg/native-crates (bridge; runs cargo build/test for pure crates first)
├── native/                      ← thin #[napi] bindings (+ build.rs)
└── shared/                      ← pure logic, plain cargo test
packages/native/npm/native/      ← @myorg/native (what you import)
├── package.json  tsconfig.json  turbo.json  tests/
├── index.js  index.d.ts         ← generated by napi (loader + types)
└── native.linux-x64-gnu.node    ← generated host binary
   (npm/native-<platform>/ dirs only exist in CI, gitignored here)
```

**Dev loop:**
```bash
bun install
bun run build:native      # procs: @myorg/native-crates:build → @myorg/native:build

## Objective
- Move the Rust/native workspace from `packages/native/` to repo-root `crates/` (alongside `packages/` and `apps/`), keeping the bridge-node Turbo design (no experimental Turbo Cargo workspaces) and keeping native prunable by the scaffolder when declined.

## Important Details
- User decisions: (1) `crates/` at repo root, side by side with `packages/` + `apps/`; (2) do NOT use Turbo's `experimentalCargoWorkspaces`; (3) native must remain prunable during scaffold cleanup (`native=none`).
- Current design (what the plan moves): root of everything Rust is `packages/native/Cargo.toml` (virtual workspace, resolver 3, members `crates/native`, `crates/shared`); bridge node `packages/native/crates/package.json` (`@myorg/native-crates`) is a real Bun workspace member with `m native ... --pure` scripts; binding npm package `packages/native/npm/native` (`@myorg/native`) depends on `@myorg/native-crates: workspace:*` so Turbo orders pure Rust before napi builds.
- AI assistant's open recommendation (awaiting user confirmation): keep the JS wrapper at `packages/native/npm/native` rather than flattening — flattening is the question the user just asked, not yet answered.
- Why `npm/native` nest exists (structural, partially confirmed via napi docs): `packages/native/` is currently the Cargo workspace root, so the npm package lives one level down under `npm/`; napi `create-npm-dirs` generates per-platform sibling packages (e.g. `native-darwin-arm64/`) inside the same npm dir; flattening the npm package to `packages/native/` would put generated per-platform dirs directly under the `packages/*` workspace glob.
- napi-rs manual setup docs describe exactly this monorepo pattern: workspace `Cargo.toml` + `crates/...` + npm package dir, driven by `napi build --cwd ... --manifest-path ... --package ... --package-json-path ... --output-dir ...`; `@napi-rs/cli@^3` is a devDependency of `@myorg/tooling`.
- Turbo 2.x experimental flag `futureFlags.experimentalCargoWorkspaces` exists (discover crates as graph nodes, maps build/test/lint/format to cargo) but requires root Cargo.toml + `[workspace.metadata] name` + cargo on PATH, and is explicitly experimental — user rejected it.
- Planned new layout: `./Cargo.toml`, `./rust-toolchain.toml`, `./.cargo/config.toml`, `./crates/` (bridge `package.json`, `turbo.json`, `native/`, `shared/`), `./packages/native/npm/native` unchanged; root workspaces `"crates"` + `"packages/native/npm/*"`.
- Bridge `crates/turbo.json` inputs (`../Cargo.toml`, `*/src/**/*.rs`, ...) are byte-identical after the move (bridge stays one level below the Cargo root).
- `crates/native/Cargo.toml` (cdylib, `napi.workspace`, `shared.workspace`) and `crates/shared/Cargo.toml` (pure, no napi) are just path-depth-agnostic workspace members — only the workspace root and npm-side depths change.
- Keep `[workspace.lints.rust] unsafe_code = "deny"` NOT `forbid` (napi expands to `unsafe`; forbid breaks compile).
- `rust-toolchain.toml` pins channel only — never components/targets (rustup refuses all cargo commands if a demanded component is missing; CI installs clippy/rustfmt/wasm32-wasip1-threads explicitly).
- `mnative` commands: `list`, `matrix --gha`, `add <name> [--pure]`, `sync`, `build/check/clippy/fmt/fmt:check/test` (+ `--pure`), `napi:build[:debug|:wasm] --only <pkg>`, `artifacts --dir`, `create-npm-dirs`. `sync` reconciles Cargo path deps ↔ `workspace:*` edges.
- Scaffolder native feature (features.ts): select none/publish/docker; `none` removes `packages/native`, `apps/example/src/pages/api/native`, scripts `build:native|build:wasm|test:native|security:audit`, turbo tasks `build:native|build:wasm`; `reconcileWorkspaces` auto-drops globs/`workspace:*` pointing at pruned dirs.
- CI: workflows are generated (`bun run docs:sync`); fragments under `packages/tooling/src/ci/{fragments,sections}/native*` use `{{NATIVE_DIR}}`, `{{NATIVE_CARGO}}`, `{{NATIVE_NPM}}` placeholders; guard on `hashFiles('Cargo.toml')` after the move.
- Known gap (CONTEXT.md): per-platform native npm publish ordering unwired — `native.yml` uploads `native-npm-packages` artifact but nothing consumes it yet.
- Sandbox constraints: no Rust toolchain (cargo/napi builds no-op — structure tests only), no Playwright browsers (e2e skips).

## Objective
- Move the Rust/native workspace from `packages/native/` to the repo root: `crates/` alongside `packages/` and `apps/`, with the Cargo workspace root, `rust-toolchain.toml`, and `.cargo/` at `./`. Keep the existing bridge-node design (`@myorg/native-crates` as a Bun workspace package whose `m native ... --pure` scripts stand for all pure crates) — Turbo's `experimentalCargoWorkspaces` is rejected. Native stays prunable when the scaffolder's `native=none` option is chosen.
- Answer the user's two follow-up questions before finalizing the plan: (1) can `packages/native/npm/native` be flattened to `packages/native/npm` or `packages/native`; (2) what does consuming `@myorg/native` look like in practice.

## Important Details
- User decisions: repo-root `crates/` co-located with `packages/` + `apps/`; no experimental Turbo (stable bridge node); scaffold cleanup must still prune native (Cargo root, crates, toolchain, npm packages) when declined.
- Current layout being moved: `packages/native/Cargo.toml` (virtual workspace, resolver 3, members `crates/native` + `crates/shared`), `packages/native/crates/` (bridge `package.json` + `turbo.json`), `packages/native/npm/native/` (`@myorg/native`), plus `rust-toolchain.toml`, `.cargo/config.toml`, `.gitignore`. Root `package.json` workspaces: `["apps/*", "packages/*", "packages/native/npm/*", "packages/native/crates"]`.
- Target layout: `./Cargo.toml`, `./crates/{package.json,turbo.json,native/,shared/}`, `./rust-toolchain.toml`, `./.cargo/config.toml`, `./packages/native/npm/native` unchanged (root workspaces become `"crates"` + `"packages/native/npm/*"`).
- Bridge `crates/turbo.json` inputs (`../Cargo.toml`, `*/src/**/*.rs`, `../Cargo.lock`, `../rust-toolchain.toml`) are byte-identical after the move because the bridge stays one level below the Cargo root; only `npm/native/turbo.json` input depths change (`../../…` → `../../../../…`).
- Crate manifests are path-agnostic: `crates/native/Cargo.toml` (cdylib, `napi.workspace`, `shared.workspace`, build-dep `napi-build.workspace`), `crates/shared/Cargo.toml` (pure, no deps); lazy-cent: `[workspace.dependencies]` pins `napi = { version = "3", features = ["napi4", "async"] }`, `napi-derive = "3"`, `napi-build = "2"`, `shared = { path = "crates/shared" }`.
- Do not change `[workspace.lints.rust] unsafe_code = "deny"` to `forbid` (napi expands to `unsafe`; forbid breaks compilation); keep `[workspace.lints.clippy]` all-warn and `[profile.release]`/`[profile.ci]`.
- `rust-toolchain.toml` deliberately pins channel only — never components/targets (rustup refuses *all* cargo commands if a demanded piece is missing; CI installs clippy/rustfmt/wasm32-wasip1-threads explicitly).
- Flattening question — facts that bear on it: (a) `packages/native/` is currently the Cargo workspace root, which is what forces the JS package one level down under `npm/`; (b) napi `create-npm-dirs` emits per-platform sibling package dirs (e.g. `native-darwin-arm64/`, gitignored, CI-only artifacts — see `native.yml` upload globs `packages/native/npm/*/*.node` + `.dockerignore` line `packages/native/npm/*-*/`) inside the npm dir; (c) after the Cargo root moves to `./`, nothing else owns `packages/native/`, so the package *could* physically move up, but every CI glob, Dockerfile copy, gitignore entry, test expectation, and the scaffold prune keyed to the current shape would have to follow. The assistant's recommendation (still unconfirmed by the user): keep `packages/native/npm/<binding>`.
- Platform artifacts split (established earlier): local dev = host build only (`m native napi:build:debug` writes `*.node` + `index.js` + `index.d.ts` into the package dir); per-platform packages are CI-only artifacts, never committed; WASM build gated on `WASI_SDK_PATH`; `@myorg/native` symlinks from `node_modules` → `packages/native/npm/native` (verified working).
- Usage pattern: `apps/example`'s `/api/native/*` routes (add, fibonacci, primes, reverse, status) and `packages/external/src/native.ts` consume `@myorg/native`; `@myorg/external` keeps a JS fallback so a missing `.node` never hard-fails. `apps/example` is unbundled (imports `@myorg/external` only, never `@myorg/internal`).

# Pixi in a Rust Monorepo — Arena.ai Sandbox Integration Guide

---

## Mental Model

Think of it as **two separate concerns that never mix:**

```
CONCERN 1: The environment          CONCERN 2: Your code
─────────────────────────           ──────────────────────
pixi.toml defines tools             Cargo.toml defines deps
pixi.lock pins exact versions       Cargo.lock pins exact versions
pixi-pack ships the environment     cargo build ships your software
conda-forge provides binaries       crates.io provides libraries
```

The environment is **versioned and released independently** from your code. When you update `rustc`, you cut a new environment release. When you update a crate, you just commit `Cargo.lock`. They never block each other.

The sandbox gets **one tarball** that contains everything it needs to build, lint, and test locally — rust toolchain, actionlint, act, podman. No apt, no brew, no internet inside the sandbox.

---

## Repository Layout

Your monorepo has one `pixi.toml` at the root. It defines feature groups that map to what different roles need:

- **`default`** — rust toolchain only, for building
- **`ci`** — adds actionlint + act + podman, for local CI testing
- **`full`** — everything, for human developers

The workspace `Cargo.toml` and `pixi.toml` sit side by side at root. The `.pixi/` directory is gitignored. The `pixi.lock` is **committed** — it is your reproducibility guarantee, exactly like `Cargo.lock`.

---

## CI Flow (on the internet-connected side)

There are two distinct CI pipelines and it's critical not to conflate them:

```
PIPELINE 1: Pack the environment (runs rarely)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Trigger: pixi.toml or pixi.lock changes
Machine: Standard GitHub Actions runner (has internet)
Steps:   pixi-pack × (environment × platform) matrix
Output:  Release assets on your repo's releases page
Cost:    ~5 minutes, runs maybe once a week

PIPELINE 2: Build and test your code (runs constantly)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Trigger: Every push, every PR
Machine: Arena.ai sandbox (no internet, or restricted)
Steps:   Download env tarball → unpack → cargo build → cargo test
Input:   Release asset URL from Pipeline 1
Cost:    ~90 seconds warm, your code only
```

Pipeline 1 produces the environment. Pipeline 2 consumes it. The agent only ever participates in Pipeline 2.

---

## Download Flow (inside the sandbox)

Three sequential fetches, then fully offline:

```
1. pixi binary          ← github.com/prefix-dev/pixi/releases
                          static musl binary, ~30MB, cached forever

2. environment tarball  ← github.com/your-org/your-repo/releases
                          contains rust + actionlint + act + podman
                          versioned by your release tag, ~400MB

3. (optional) act image ← pre-pulled and embedded or skipped
                          act can run without Docker for lint-only

──────────────── NO MORE NETWORK BELOW THIS LINE ────────────────

unpack → activate → cargo build → actionlint → act
```

The environment tarball URL is the **only thing that changes between sandbox setups**. Everything else — the unpack procedure, the activation, the build commands — is identical across every agent run. This is what the agent prompt encodes.

---

## Two-Stage Bootstrap via Pixi Tasks

There's a subtle but powerful refinement to the download flow: **only the pixi binary needs to be fetched by a raw shell command. Everything after that can be a `pixi task`.**

### The Insight

The environment tarball fetch is itself a scripted operation with inputs (URL, tag, platform, checksum), outputs (extracted directory, activate.sh), and error paths (checksum mismatch, wrong platform). That's exactly what `pixi task` is for. Once you have the `pixi` binary, you have a task runner — even before the environment is unpacked.

This lets you split bootstrap into two stages with different characteristics:

```
STAGE 1: Get pixi         (raw shell, ~5 seconds)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
curl one binary → chmod +x → done.
No dependencies. No task runner needed.
This is the ONLY step the agent memorizes.

STAGE 2: Get environment  (pixi task, ~60 seconds)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
pixi run fetch-env
Reads ENV_TAG from env var or pixi config.
Handles URL construction, download, checksum, unpack, activation prep.
Fully declared in pixi.toml — versioned with the repo.
```

### Why This Matters

**The agent prompt gets simpler.** Instead of encoding curl invocations for the environment tarball, checksum verification, platform detection, and unpack flags, the prompt just says: *"Fetch pixi, then run `pixi run fetch-env`."* All the fetch logic lives in `pixi.toml` where it can be reviewed, versioned, and updated without changing the agent prompt.

**The fetch logic is testable locally.** Any developer with pixi installed can run `pixi run fetch-env` to reproduce exactly what the agent does. No secret sandbox behavior, no drift between "what the docs say" and "what the agent actually runs."

**Platform detection moves out of the prompt.** A `pixi task` runs with a shell and can inspect `uname -m` / `uname -s` to pick the right asset. The agent prompt no longer needs a platform table.

**Checksum enforcement is guaranteed.** The task always runs `sha256sum --check`. There's no path where the agent "forgets" to verify, because the task fails if verification fails.

### Task Definitions

Add these to `pixi.toml`:

```toml
[tasks.fetch-env]
description = "Download and unpack the packed agent environment"
cmd = """
set -euo pipefail

: "${ENV_TAG:?ENV_TAG must be set (e.g. env-2025.07.01)}"
: "${PIXI_ENVIRONMENT:=full}"

REPO="your-org/your-repo"
BASE="https://github.com/${REPO}/releases/download/${ENV_TAG}"

# Platform detection
case "$(uname -s)-$(uname -m)" in
  Linux-x86_64)   PLATFORM="linux-64"      ;;
  Linux-aarch64)  PLATFORM="linux-aarch64" ;;
  Darwin-x86_64)  PLATFORM="osx-64"        ;;
  Darwin-arm64)   PLATFORM="osx-arm64"     ;;
  *) echo "Unsupported platform: $(uname -s)-$(uname -m)"; exit 1 ;;
esac

mkdir -p .tools
cd .tools

echo "→ Fetching env asset for ${PLATFORM} @ ${ENV_TAG}"
curl -fsSL "${BASE}/agent-${PIXI_ENVIRONMENT}-${PLATFORM}.sh" -o env.sh
curl -fsSL "${BASE}/SHA256SUMS"                               -o SHA256SUMS

echo "→ Verifying checksum"
sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS

echo "→ Unpacking"
chmod +x env.sh
./env.sh --output-directory env

echo "✓ Environment ready. Source .tools/env/activate.sh to activate."
"""

[tasks.verify-env]
description = "Sanity-check that all expected tools are on PATH"
cmd = """
set -euo pipefail
for tool in cargo rustc actionlint act podman; do
  if command -v "$tool" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "✓ $tool: $($tool --version 2>&1 | head -1)"
  else
    echo "✗ $tool: MISSING"; exit 1
  fi
done
"""

[tasks.bootstrap]
description = "One-shot: fetch env + verify"
depends-on = ["fetch-env", "verify-env"]
```

### Revised Bootstrap Sequence

The agent's operational script becomes:

```bash
# Stage 1: get pixi (raw shell, unavoidable)
curl -fsSL "${PIXI_URL}" -o pixi && chmod +x pixi

# Stage 2: hand off to pixi tasks (all logic lives in pixi.toml)
export ENV_TAG="env-2025.07.01"
export PIXI_ENVIRONMENT="full"
./pixi run bootstrap

# Activate for the session
source .tools/env/activate.sh
```

Four lines. That's the entire prompt-side bootstrap. Everything else — URL construction, platform detection, checksum verification, unpack, sanity checks — is versioned code in `pixi.toml`.

### When You'd Skip This

If you have exactly one platform, one environment, and no checksum discipline, the two-stage split is overkill and you should just curl-and-unpack inline. But the moment you have two platforms *or* two environment flavors *or* want checksums enforced, the pixi-task approach pays for itself immediately.

---

## How act + podman Fits In

`act` runs your `.github/workflows/` locally by spawning containers. Inside the sandbox:

- **podman** is the container runtime, available in the pixi environment
- **act** is configured to use podman via `DOCKER_HOST`
- The activation script (produced by pixi-unpack) sets up this wiring automatically
- Net result: `act push` inside the sandbox is equivalent to pushing to GitHub

The key insight: because both `act` and `podman` came from conda-forge into the same pixi environment, their paths and library dependencies are already coherent. No manual wiring beyond a config file.

For actionlint you don't need podman at all — it's a pure static binary that parses workflow YAML. Run it before act as a fast pre-check.

---

## Agent Prompt

Give the agent exactly this context block in the system prompt or SETUP_TASK:

```
ENVIRONMENT SETUP
─────────────────
This is an offline sandbox. All tools arrive via a pre-packed pixi environment.

Environment version: {ENV_TAG}           ← operator fills this in
Pixi URL:            {PIXI_URL}          ← operator fills this in

BOOTSTRAP (run exactly once at session start):
  1. curl -fsSL "${PIXI_URL}" -o pixi && chmod +x pixi
  2. export ENV_TAG="{ENV_TAG}"
  3. ./pixi run bootstrap
  4. source .tools/env/activate.sh

The `bootstrap` task handles URL construction, platform detection,
checksum verification, unpack, and tool sanity checks. If it fails,
report the exact output — do NOT attempt to fetch or install manually.

AFTER BOOTSTRAP you have available:
  cargo, rustc, rust-analyzer     — build and check Rust code
  actionlint                      — lint .github/workflows/*.yml
  act                             — run GitHub Actions workflows locally
  podman                          — container runtime for act

WORKFLOW TESTING:
  - Always run actionlint before act
  - act uses podman automatically, no Docker needed
  - Use `act -n` for dry-run if you only want to see the plan

DO NOT:
  - Run apt, brew, cargo install, pip install, or curl to anything
    other than the pixi binary URL given above
  - Assume git, jq, unzip, or brotli are available
  - Attempt to install system packages
  - Bypass `pixi run bootstrap` by fetching the env tarball directly
```

---

## Key Invariants the Agent Must Understand

**One source of truth per concern:**
- Environment version lives in `ENV_TAG`, not in code
- Rust dependency versions live in `Cargo.lock`, not in the environment
- Workflow correctness is validated by actionlint, then act — in that order
- Fetch logic lives in `pixi.toml` tasks, not in the agent prompt

**The environment is immutable from the agent's perspective:**
- If a tool is missing, the fix is a new environment release, not `cargo install` or `apt install`
- The agent should report missing tools as environment gaps, not fix them ad-hoc

**Activation is a session-level operation:**
- Done once at session start
- All subsequent commands inherit the activated environment
- The agent should never re-activate mid-session

**act is a local truth proxy, not ground truth:**
- act + podman approximates GitHub Actions but isn't identical
- Divergence (different runner image, secrets unavailable) is expected and normal
- The agent's job is to get act passing, not to guarantee CI passing

**The pixi binary is the only "raw fetch."**
- Once pixi exists, all further download and setup logic is a task
- This keeps the agent prompt small and the fetch logic in version control


## Manually Dispatchable Bundle Environment CI

### Mental Model

The bundle environment pipeline is **not a reaction to code changes** — it's a deliberate operator decision. You are cutting a new version of the environment, the same way you'd cut a library release. It should require a human to pull the trigger, not fire automatically on every commit to `pixi.toml`.

```
WRONG mental model:   pixi.toml changes → auto-rebuild environment
RIGHT mental model:   operator decides  → rebuild environment → new tag
```

This distinction matters because environment rebuilds are expensive (~5 min × platform matrix), affect every downstream agent session, and should be intentional. A stray whitespace change to `pixi.toml` should not silently ship a new environment to all agents.

---

### Workflow Structure

The workflow has three inputs the operator fills in at dispatch time:

- **`env_tag`** — the release tag to publish under, e.g. `env-2025.07.01`. Distinct from your code release tags. Operators bump this when they want agents to notice.
- **`environment`** — which pixi environment to pack: `default`, `ci`, or `full`. Allows targeted rebuilds without rebuilding everything.
- **`platforms`** — comma-separated list of target platforms. Lets you rebuild only `linux-aarch64` if that's what changed.

The workflow itself does exactly four things in sequence: resolves the lockfile, runs the platform matrix in parallel, publishes assets to a GitHub release under `env_tag`, and posts a summary of what was built and what SHA256 each asset has.

---

### Trigger Philosophy

Three legitimate reasons to manually dispatch:

```
1. You changed pixi.toml          → new package, version bump, new feature group
2. conda-forge upstream changed    → a package got a security patch you want to pull in
3. You're adding a new platform    → linux-aarch64 support, for example
```

One illegitimate reason that will bite you:

```
✗ You dispatch because you're not sure if the current env is good
  → fix this by trusting pixi.lock and the SHA256 summary instead
```

---

### Release Asset Naming Convention

Assets land on your repo's releases page under `env_tag` with names that encode everything the agent needs to select the right one:

```
agent-{environment}-{platform}-{env_tag}.sh

examples:
  agent-full-linux-64-env-2025.07.01.sh
  agent-full-linux-aarch64-env-2025.07.01.sh
  agent-ci-linux-64-env-2025.07.01.sh
```

The agent prompt receives `ENV_TAG` from the operator. The `fetch-env` pixi task constructs the URL deterministically from that tag + its own detected platform. No manifest lookup needed.

---

### Lockfile Discipline

The dispatch workflow should **fail fast if `pixi.lock` is not committed and up to date**. This enforces the invariant that the lock always reflects the manifest. The correct flow is:

```
developer locally:  edit pixi.toml → pixi install (updates lock) → commit both
operator:           sees committed lock → dispatches workflow
CI:                 runs pixi-pack --frozen (never re-solves, uses committed lock)
```

If the workflow re-solved the lockfile itself during CI, you'd get non-reproducible environment builds. The lock is solved once, locally, deliberately, then frozen for all subsequent packing.

---

### Integration with Agent Prompt

The operator updates exactly one line in the agent system prompt after each dispatch:

```
Before:  Environment version: env-2025.06.15
After:   Environment version: env-2025.07.01
```

That single change propagates the new environment to all subsequent agent sessions. Old sessions that already bootstrapped are unaffected — they continue using whatever they unpacked. This is intentional. Environment updates are not hot-patched into running sessions.

---

### Rollback

Because every dispatch produces a tagged GitHub release, rollback is trivial:

```
Something broke in env-2025.07.01?
→ operator changes ENV_TAG back to env-2025.06.15 in agent prompt
→ done, no rebuild needed, old assets still exist on releases page
```

This is the main reason environment release tags must be immutable and never force-pushed over.


```yaml
# .github/workflows/pack-agent-env.yml

name: Pack Agent Environment

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      env_tag:
        description: "Release tag  —  e.g. env-2025.07.01"
        required: true
        type: string
      environment:
        description: "Pixi environment to pack"
        required: true
        type: choice
        default: full
        options:
          - full
          - ci
          - default
      platforms:
        description: "Target platforms (comma-separated)"
        required: true
        default: "linux-64,linux-aarch64"
        type: string

env:
  PIXI_VERSION:      v0.48.0
  PIXI_PACK_VERSION: v0.7.10

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
jobs:

# ── Job 1: Validate lockfile, compute platform matrix ─────────────────────────
  setup:
    name: Validate lockfile + build matrix
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      matrix: ${{ steps.matrix.outputs.value }}

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: prefix-dev/setup-pixi@v0.8.1
        with:
          pixi-version: ${{ env.PIXI_VERSION }}
          frozen: true          # fails immediately if lock is stale

      - name: Assert lockfile is committed and current
        run: pixi install --frozen --environment ${{ inputs.environment }}

      - name: Build platform matrix from input string
        id: matrix
        run: |
          json=$(echo "${{ inputs.platforms }}" \
                 | tr ',' '\n' \
                 | sed 's/^ *//;s/ *$//' \
                 | jq -R . \
                 | jq -sc .)
          echo "value={\"platform\":${json}}" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT


# ── Job 2: Pack one self-extracting .sh per platform (parallel) ───────────────
  pack:
    name: Pack / ${{ matrix.platform }}
    needs: setup
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix: ${{ fromJson(needs.setup.outputs.matrix) }}

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # pixi-pack runs on the CI runner (always linux-64)
      - name: Download pixi-pack (build-host binary)
        run: |
          curl -fsSL \
            "https://github.com/quantco/pixi-pack/releases/download/${{ env.PIXI_PACK_VERSION }}/pixi-pack-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl" \
            -o pixi-pack
          chmod +x pixi-pack

      # pixi-unpack is EMBEDDED inside the .sh for the TARGET platform
      - name: Download pixi-unpack (target-platform binary)
        run: |
          case "${{ matrix.platform }}" in
            linux-64)      TARGET="x86_64-unknown-linux-musl"  ;;
            linux-aarch64) TARGET="aarch64-unknown-linux-musl" ;;
            osx-64)        TARGET="x86_64-apple-darwin"        ;;
            osx-arm64)     TARGET="aarch64-apple-darwin"       ;;
            *)
              echo "Unsupported platform: ${{ matrix.platform }}"
              exit 1
              ;;
          esac
          curl -fsSL \
            "https://github.com/quantco/pixi-pack/releases/download/${{ env.PIXI_PACK_VERSION }}/pixi-unpack-${TARGET}" \
            -o pixi-unpack-target
          chmod +x pixi-unpack-target

      # Also download the pixi binary for the target so agents fetch
      # everything from one release page (your repo, not prefix-dev)
      - name: Download pixi binary (target-platform)
        run: |
          case "${{ matrix.platform }}" in
            linux-64)      TARGET="x86_64-unknown-linux-musl"  ;;
            linux-aarch64) TARGET="aarch64-unknown-linux-musl" ;;
            osx-64)        TARGET="x86_64-apple-darwin"        ;;
            osx-arm64)     TARGET="aarch64-apple-darwin"       ;;
          esac
          curl -fsSL \
            "https://github.com/prefix-dev/pixi/releases/download/${{ env.PIXI_VERSION }}/pixi-${TARGET}" \
            -o "pixi-${{ matrix.platform }}"
          chmod +x "pixi-${{ matrix.platform }}"

      - name: Pack environment → self-extracting .sh
        run: |
          ./pixi-pack pack \
            --manifest-path       pixi.toml \
            --environment         ${{ inputs.environment }} \
            --platform            ${{ matrix.platform }} \
            --create-executable \
            --pixi-unpack-source  ./pixi-unpack-target \
            --output-file         agent-${{ inputs.environment }}-${{ matrix.platform }}.sh

      - name: Compute SHA256 checksums
        run: |
          sha256sum \
            agent-${{ inputs.environment }}-${{ matrix.platform }}.sh \
            pixi-${{ matrix.platform }} \
            > checksums-${{ matrix.platform }}.sha256
          cat checksums-${{ matrix.platform }}.sha256   # visible in log

      - name: Upload artifacts for release job
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: assets-${{ matrix.platform }}
          retention-days: 1
          path: |
            agent-*.sh
            pixi-*
            checksums-*.sha256


# ── Job 3: Create GitHub Release, upload all assets ───────────────────────────
  release:
    name: Publish release ${{ inputs.env_tag }}
    needs: pack
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write

    steps:
      - name: Download all packed artifacts
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          pattern: assets-*
          merge-multiple: true

      - name: Merge checksum files
        run: cat checksums-*.sha256 > SHA256SUMS

      - name: Create GitHub Release
        uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v2
        with:
          tag_name:   ${{ inputs.env_tag }}
          name:       "Agent Environment ${{ inputs.env_tag }}"
          make_latest: false
          body: |
            ## Agent Environment — `${{ inputs.env_tag }}`

            | Field | Value |
            |---|---|
            | **Pixi environment** | `${{ inputs.environment }}` |
            | **Platforms** | `${{ inputs.platforms }}` |
            | **Pixi version** | `${{ env.PIXI_VERSION }}` |
            | **pixi-pack version** | `${{ env.PIXI_PACK_VERSION }}` |
            | **Packed by** | @${{ github.actor }} |
            | **Commit** | ${{ github.sha }} |

            ### Asset naming

            ```
            agent-{environment}-{platform}.sh   ← self-extracting, run directly
            pixi-{platform}                     ← static pixi binary
            SHA256SUMS                          ← checksums for all assets
            ```

            ### Agent prompt update

            Change exactly one line in the agent system prompt:
            ```
            Environment version: ${{ inputs.env_tag }}
            ```

            ### Bootstrap (copy-paste into SETUP_TASK.md)

            ```bash
            # Stage 1: fetch pixi (raw)
            PLATFORM="linux-64"   # or linux-aarch64
            BASE="https://github.com/${{ github.repository }}/releases/download/${{ inputs.env_tag }}"
            curl -fsSL "${BASE}/pixi-${PLATFORM}" -o pixi && chmod +x pixi

            # Stage 2: hand off to pixi tasks
            export ENV_TAG="${{ inputs.env_tag }}"
            export PIXI_ENVIRONMENT="${{ inputs.environment }}"
            ./pixi run bootstrap

            # Activate
            source .tools/env/activate.sh
            ```
          files: |
            agent-*.sh
            pixi-*
            SHA256SUMS


# ── Job 4: Step summary (checksums + prompt snippet) ─────────────────────────
  summary:
    name: Write job summary
    needs: [setup, pack, release]
    if: always()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Download all packed artifacts
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          pattern: assets-*
          merge-multiple: true

      - name: Write summary
        run: |
          {
            echo "## 📦 Agent Environment Pack — \`${{ inputs.env_tag }}\`"
            echo ""
            echo "| | |"
            echo "|---|---|"
            echo "| **Tag** | \`${{ inputs.env_tag }}\` |"
            echo "| **Environment** | \`${{ inputs.environment }}\` |"
            echo "| **Platforms** | \`${{ inputs.platforms }}\` |"
            echo "| **Triggered by** | @${{ github.actor }} |"
            echo "| **Commit** | \`${{ github.sha }}\` |"
            echo ""
            echo "### Assets and checksums"
            echo ""
            echo "| Asset | SHA256 |"
            echo "|---|---|"
            while IFS= read -r line; do
              sha=$(echo "$line" | awk '{print $1}')
              file=$(echo "$line" | awk '{print $2}')
              echo "| \`${file}\` | \`${sha}\` |"
            done < <(cat checksums-*.sha256)
            echo ""
            echo "### Paste into agent system prompt"
            echo '```'
            echo "Environment version: ${{ inputs.env_tag }}"
            echo '```'
            echo ""

            # Emit a clear warning if any upstream job failed
            if [[ "${{ needs.pack.result }}" != "success" || \
                  "${{ needs.release.result }}" != "success" ]]; then
              echo "---"
              echo "> ⚠️ **One or more jobs failed.** Release may be incomplete."
              echo "> Check the pack and release job logs above."
            fi
          } >> $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY
```

---

## What Each Job Does

```
setup    Checks pixi.lock is committed + current.
         Converts the platforms input string into a JSON matrix.
         Fails immediately if lock is stale — before any compute runs.

pack     Runs in parallel, one runner per platform.
         Downloads pixi-pack (build-host, always linux-64).
         Downloads pixi-unpack for the TARGET platform → embeds in .sh.
         Downloads the pixi binary for the TARGET platform → release asset.
         Runs pixi-pack --create-executable → fully self-contained .sh.
         Computes SHA256 for all assets.

release  Merges all per-platform artifacts.
         Creates a GitHub Release under env_tag.
         Uploads: agent-*.sh, pixi-*, SHA256SUMS.
         Body contains the exact bootstrap snippet agents copy-paste.

summary  Writes the job summary table with all checksums.
         Emits the exact one-liner the operator pastes into agent prompts.
         Reports clearly if any job failed, so partial releases are obvious.
```

---

## Three Callouts Worth Noting

**Agents only ever hit your repo's release page.** Both the `pixi` binary and the environment `.sh` are published as your release assets. No agent fetches from `prefix-dev` or `quantco` at runtime — that happens once, on the CI runner, during the pack job.

**`frozen: true` in `setup-pixi` is the lockfile guard.** If a developer edits `pixi.toml` and forgets to run `pixi install` locally before pushing, the setup job fails in under 30 seconds before any expensive matrix work starts. The fix is always the same: run `pixi install` locally, commit the updated `pixi.lock`, repush.

**The agent prompt only mentions `pixi run bootstrap`, not the env URL.** The `fetch-env` task inside `pixi.toml` is the single source of truth for how the environment tarball is located, downloaded, verified, and unpacked. Changing fetch behavior (new mirror, new checksum scheme, new unpack directory) is a `pixi.toml` edit, not a prompt edit. This is what makes the two-stage bootstrap durable.

## Crate Sources as a Separate Release (Cargo Vendor)

### Why Not Inside the Pixi Env

The pixi env carries the **toolchain** (`rustc`, `cargo`, linker). Crate sources are a different concern with a different update cadence:

```
Pixi env:   updates quarterly (new rustc)      → manual dispatch
Vendor tar: updates per Cargo.lock change       → automatic on merge
```

Bundling crates into the pixi env would force a 400MB env rebuild every time a dependency bumps. Keeping them separate preserves the two-pipeline model and lets each tarball evolve independently.

---

### Architecture

Three release artifacts, three independent lifecycles:

```
Artifact              Trigger                  Size      Update frequency
────────────────────  ───────────────────────  ────────  ────────────────
pixi-{platform}       pixi env dispatch        ~30MB     quarterly
agent-env-{tag}.sh    pixi env dispatch        ~400MB    quarterly
vendor-{lockhash}.tar Cargo.lock change        ~50-300MB per dep bump
```

The sandbox bootstrap fetches all three, then goes fully offline.

---

### Vendor CI Pipeline

**Trigger:** Push to `main` where `Cargo.lock` changed. Can be fully automatic — unlike the pixi env dispatch, vendor rebuilds are cheap (~2 min, single platform, no matrix) and idempotent.

**Steps:**
1. Checkout repo
2. `cargo vendor vendor-tmp/`
3. Tar + zstd compress → `vendor-{sha256_of_Cargo.lock}.tar.zst`
4. Publish as GitHub release asset under a rolling `vendor-latest` tag (or a `vendor-{date}` tag)

**Key detail:** The release tag encodes the `Cargo.lock` hash, not a date. This makes it deterministic — two CI runs on the same lock produce the same tag and skip the upload if the asset already exists.

**Naming:** `vendor-{lockhash_short}-{platform}.tar.zst`

---

### Bootstrap Changes

The `fetch-env` pixi task gains a sibling:

```
fetch-env       → downloads + unpacks toolchain tar
fetch-vendor    → downloads + unpacks vendor tar into vendor/
bootstrap       → depends-on: [fetch-env, fetch-vendor, verify-env]
```

`fetch-vendor` reads `VENDOR_TAG` (or derives it from `sha256sum Cargo.lock`), fetches the tar, extracts to `./vendor/`, and verifies the directory is non-empty.

The repo ships a `.cargo/config.toml` pointing at `vendor/`:

```toml
[source.crates-io]
replace-with = "vendored-sources"
[source.vendored-sources]
directory = "vendor"
```

This file is committed. It works identically whether `vendor/` was populated by `cargo vendor` locally or by unpacking the release tar in the sandbox.

---

### Agent Prompt Update

Two new variables, one new bootstrap step:

```
Environment version: {ENV_TAG}
Vendor version:      {VENDOR_TAG}      ← lock hash or date tag
Pixi URL:            {PIXI_URL}

BOOTSTRAP:
  1. curl pixi binary
  2. export ENV_TAG VENDOR_TAG
  3. ./pixi run bootstrap          ← fetches env AND vendor
  4. source .tools/env/activate.sh
  5. cargo build --offline
```

---

### Key Invariants

- **No `vendor/` in git.** The repo stays lean. Vendor sources arrive at bootstrap time from the release tar.
- **`Cargo.lock` hash is the vendor tag.** Deterministic, no human decision needed, auto-derivable.
- **Vendor CI is automatic, pixi env CI is manual.** Different risk profiles — a bad vendor tar breaks one build and rolls forward on next lock change; a bad env tar breaks every agent session.
- **`cargo build --offline` is mandatory in the sandbox.** If it tries to reach crates.io, something is wrong with the vendor tar or `.cargo/config.toml`. Fail loud.
- **Local dev path unchanged.** Developers with internet run `cargo vendor` themselves or just let cargo fetch normally (the source replacement still works if `vendor/` exists locally). The release tar is only for the sandbox.

---

### Rollback

Same model as the pixi env: change `VENDOR_TAG` in the agent prompt to a previous lock hash. Old vendor tars are immutable release assets. No rebuild needed.


# Prebuild Playwright Chromium in GitHub Actions

 If you want to **download a ready-to-use Playwright Chromium build from a GitHub Release**, the basic approach is:

 1. Install Chromium with Playwright.
2. Put the Playwright browser directory into a ZIP.
3. Upload the ZIP as a GitHub Actions artifact and/or Release asset.
4. Users can download the ZIP without running `npx playwright install`.

 Playwright stores downloaded browsers in an OS-specific cache directory, but you can make this predictable by setting `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH`.  Playwright

 ### Example workflow

```
name: Build Playwright Chromium

on:
  push:
    tags:
      - "v*"

permissions:
  contents: write

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v6
        with:
          node-version: lts/*

      - run: npm ci

      # Install only Chromium into a predictable directory
      - name: Install Chromium
        run: npx playwright install chromium
        env:
          PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH: ./pw-browsers

      # Package the browser
      - name: Create archive
        run: |
          tar -czf playwright-chromium-linux-x64.tar.gz pw-browsers

      # Keep it available from the Actions run
      - name: Upload artifact
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v5
        with:
          name: playwright-chromium-linux-x64
          path: playwright-chromium-linux-x64.tar.gz

      # Attach it to the GitHub Release
      - name: Upload Release asset
        run: |
          gh release upload "${GITHUB_REF_NAME}" \
            playwright-chromium-linux-x64.tar.gz
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
```

 Playwright officially supports installing a specific browser with `npx playwright install chromium`; `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH` lets you control where the browser is installed.  Playwright

 ### Downloading it

 After pushing a tag such as:

```
git tag v1.0.0
git push origin v1.0.0
```

 the workflow produces:

```
playwright-chromium-linux-x64.tar.gz
```

 as a **GitHub Release asset**, so users can download it directly from the Release page. GitHub also supports uploading binary files such as `.zip`/`.tar.gz` as release assets.  GitHub Docs

 ### Important distinction

 If the goal is a **public downloadable release**, use a **Release asset**, not only `actions/upload-artifact`.

 - **Artifact** → primarily for files produced by a workflow run; access/retention is tied to GitHub Actions.  GitHub Docs+1
- **Release asset** → attached to a version such as `v1.0.0`, making it suitable for distributing your prebuilt Chromium.

 Also note that this example builds a **Linux Chromium bundle**. For Windows and macOS you generally want separate GitHub Actions jobs/runners and separate archives, because Playwright's browser binaries are OS-specific.  Playwright
