/** How a generated workflow should be treated on this pass. */
type WorkflowOutcome = "generate" | "remove" | "skip";

/** Which features are on — computed once, read by every spec. */
interface WorkflowContext {
  /** The `pages` feature is enabled. */
  pages: boolean;
  /** The `coverage` feature is enabled. */
  coverage: boolean;
  /** The `native` feature is enabled. */
  native: boolean;
  /** The `dependabot` or `gh-actions` feature is enabled. */
  dependabot: boolean;
  /** The `stale` feature is enabled. */
  stale: boolean;
  /** The template's own docs site deploys Pages — never true inside a scaffold. */
  templateDocsSite: boolean;
  /** Pages owns the Pages site, so no standalone `pages.yml` is generated. */
  pagesDeploysToSite: boolean;
}

/**
 * One workflow the generator owns: the skeleton it renders, the config whose
 * survival decides whether it is generated, and the stale file to clean up
 * when it is not.
 *
 * `skip` exists because an absent config is not always grounds for a cleanup —
 * a removed coverage config must not delete a `coverage.yml` that belongs to
 * something else, which is what the original `if (coverageConfigExists)` guard
 * spelled out inline.
 */
interface WorkflowSpec {
  base: string;
  steps: string;
  outcome: (ctx: WorkflowContext) => WorkflowOutcome;
  /** File to delete when the outcome is `remove`, relative to the target dir. */
  stale?: string;
  /** Parenthesised log suffix; omit it to remove silently. */
  reason?: (ctx: WorkflowContext) => string;
}

/**
 * Every workflow the repo and the scaffolds share, in generation order.
 *
 * `dependabot.base.yml` renders to `.github/dependabot.yml` rather than into
 * `.github/workflows/` — `aggregateWorkflow` derives that itself.
 */
const WORKFLOWS: readonly WorkflowSpec[] = [
  { base: "ci.base.yml", steps: "ci.steps.yml", outcome: () => "generate" },
  { base: "release.base.yml", steps: "release.steps.yml", outcome: () => "generate" },
  {
    base: "pages.base.yml",
    steps: "pages.steps.yml",
    outcome: (ctx) => (ctx.pagesDeploysToSite ? "generate" : "remove"),
    stale: ".github/workflows/pages.yml",
    reason: (ctx) => (ctx.templateDocsSite ? "template docs site deploys Pages" : "pages disabled"),
  },
  {
    base: "coverage.base.yml",
    steps: "coverage.steps.yml",

  /**
   * Applied to each rendered workflow immediately before it is written.
   *
   * Required when generating into a scaffold. The fragments ship inside this
   * package, so they arrive with their TEMPLATE-ONLY markers and `@myorg`
   * placeholders intact — and generation runs after the scaffolder's tree-wide
   * marker and scope passes, which could never reach files outside the target
   * tree anyway.
   */
  postProcess?: (rendered: string) => string;
}

/** Every feature — what an unrestricted pass (this repo, `m docs`) includes. */
function allFeatures(): ReadonlySet<string> {
  return new Set(FEATURES.map((feature) => feature.dir));
}

/** Absolute path of one `src/ci/` fragment from its registry-relative form. */
function ciPath(relative: string): string {
  return resolveSrc("ci", ...relative.split("/"));
}

/** Does this declared fragment contribute to the workflow `stepsFileName` names? */
function contributes(relative: string, stepsFileName: string): boolean {
  // CI is the odd one out: its steps are not a `<name>.steps.yml` file but a
  // `sections/<feature>.yml` chunk per feature, each carrying its own
  // `# SECTION:` marker. The WORKFLOWS spec still calls the pair
  // `ci.steps.yml`, so that name selects the whole `sections/` directory.
  if (stepsFileName === "ci.steps.yml") return relative.startsWith("sections/");
  return (relative.split("/").pop() ?? "") === stepsFileName;
}

/**
 * Every enabled feature's contribution to one workflow, in registry order.
 *
 * Registry order is alphabetical by feature dir, which is the order the old
 * `find … | sort` produced over `configs/<dir>/<steps>.yml`, so the rendered
 * workflows are byte-identical to the ones the directory scan generated.
 */
async function collectFragments(
  stepsFileName: string,
  enabled: ReadonlySet<string>,
): Promise<string[]> {
  const texts: string[] = [];
  for (const feature of FEATURES) {
    if (!enabled.has(feature.dir)) continue;
    for (const relative of feature.ciFiles ?? []) {
      if (!contributes(relative, stepsFileName)) continue;
      texts.push((await file(ciPath(relative)).text()).trimEnd());
    }
  }
  return texts;
}

/**
 * The skeleton for a workflow: whichever enabled feature declared a `ciFiles`
 * entry with this filename, or null when none did.
 */
async function resolveBase(
  baseFileName: string,
  enabled: ReadonlySet<string>,
): Promise<string | null> {
  for (const feature of FEATURES) {
    if (!enabled.has(feature.dir)) continue;
    for (const relative of feature.ciFiles ?? []) {
      if ((relative.split("/").pop() ?? "") === baseFileName) return ciPath(relative);
    }
  }
  return null;
}

/** The checkout/setup/cache/install preamble every CI job starts with. */
async function readBootstrap(): Promise<string> {
  const path = ciPath("ci.bootstrap.yml");
  if (!(await file(path).exists())) return "";
  return (await file(path).text()).trimEnd();
}

/**
 * The finishing pass a generated project needs, derived from what it recorded.
 *
 * Undefined inside this repository: its workflows keep their TEMPLATE-ONLY
 * markers and `@myorg` placeholders, because that is what makes it
 * scaffoldable.
 */
async function defaultPostProcess(
  targetDir: string,
  recorded: ConfigMap | null,
): Promise<((rendered: string) => string) | undefined> {
  if (!recorded) return undefined;

  const disabled = disabledScopesFor(FEATURES, recorded);
  const scope = await readRecordedScope(targetDir);
  return (rendered: string): string => {
    const { content } = stripMarkerBlocks(rendered, disabled);
    return scope ? content.replaceAll(DEFAULT_SCOPE, scope) : content;
  };
}

/**
 * Renders a workflow skeleton, splicing the enabled features' step fragments
 * into the `{{STEPS}}` (or `{{UPDATES}}`) placeholder.
 */
export async function aggregateWorkflow(
  targetDir: string,
  baseFileName: string,
  stepsFileName: string,
  options: AggregateOptions = {},
): Promise<void> {

/**

 * Delegates to the shared reporter so a missing cargo reads the same here as it
 * does from a Git hook or a CI step — and so the warning is always printed
 * rather than the task failing or passing silently.
 */
function cargoExistsOrWarn(): boolean {
  if (hasTool("cargo")) return true;
  skipMissingTool(TOOLS.cargo);
  return false;
}

/**
 * The native workspace is optional (`native=none` prunes it), so every cargo
 * and napi call has to be a no-op when it is absent — otherwise the root
 * scripts would need `test -f packages/native/...` guards again.
 */
function nativeExistsOrWarn(): boolean {
  if (existsSync(join(ROOT, "Cargo.toml"))) return true;
  console.warn("⚠️ Cargo.toml not present at the repo root, skipping (enable the native config)");
  return false;
}

function runCargo(args: string[], opts: { cwd?: string } = {}): number {
  if (!nativeExistsOrWarn()) return 0;
  // Reports the absent toolchain through the shared helper, so a package task
  // that shells out to cargo prints the same warning a hook would and still
  // exits 0 instead of failing the task graph.
  return withOptionalTool("cargo", () => {
    const cmd = ["cargo", ...args];
    const { exitCode, output } = spawnToolCaptured(cmd, {
      cwd: opts.cwd ?? ROOT,
    });
    if (output) process.stdout.write(output);
    // A cargo failure is the one case where "exit code 1" says nothing: the
    // reason is in the child's own stderr (a manifest error, a rustup override
    // it cannot satisfy, a compile error), so surface its tail as an annotation.
    if (exitCode !== 0) {
      annotateError(`${cmd.join(" ")} failed (exit ${exitCode})`, output);
    }
    return exitCode;
  });
}

# CONTEXT.md — packages/native

> Snapshot of this workspace's current state. Rules are in [AGENTS.md](./AGENTS.md), overview in [README.md](./README.md).

## Current state

- Virtual workspace, `resolver = "3"`, members: `crates/native` (cdylib binding) and `crates/shared` (pure Rust, no npm package).
- `crates/native` is a thin layer — every `#[napi]` fn delegates to `shared` (`shared.workspace = true`).
- `crates/package.json` (`@myorg/native-crates`) is the bridge node: the single Turbo package for all pure crates, running `mnative build/test --pure`. Root `workspaces` includes `packages/native/crates`; the binding's `package.json` depends on the bridge via `workspace:*`.
- `[workspace.package]`: edition 2024, version 0.1.0, MIT, repository `Archont561/ts-monorepo-template`.
- Shared dependencies: `napi` 3 (feature `napi4`), `napi-derive` 3, `napi-build` 2, `shared = { path = "crates/shared" }`. Lints: `unsafe_code = "forbid"`, `clippy.all = "warn"`. `[profile.release]`: lto, codegen-units 1, strip.
- Turbo: `@myorg/native#build` is **cached** (`*.node`, `index.js`, `index.d.ts`; inputs glob `../../crates/**` + workspace manifests); the bridge tasks are **never cached** (cargo owns `target/`); `build:wasm` stays uncached.
- Toolchain: stable with `rustfmt`, `clippy`, and the `wasm32-wasip1-threads` target.
- `Cargo.lock` is gitignored — these are cdylib libraries, not binaries.

## Decisions as outcomes

- **Workspace under `packages/`** — the repo root stays free of Rust, so the native config is removable as one directory.
- **One bridge package for all pure crates** — pure crates stay out of the npm namespace (no package churn when they move), while Turbo still orders pure Rust before the napi builds that consume it. The guide's per-crate npm packages were collapsed into this single node deliberately.
- **Cargo graph mirrored as `workspace:*`** — Turbo cannot see `[dependencies]` in Cargo.toml; the bridge edge is the one ordering fact it needs, and `mnative sync` keeps it honest.
- **napi builds cached, cargo tasks not** — napi outputs are stable local artifacts with well-defined inputs; cargo's incremental state is its own cache and the toolchain belongs in its key. Over-invalidating is cheap, a stale `.node` is not.
- **`unsafe_code = "deny"` inherited, not per-crate** — a new crate is safe before anyone reviews it. It has to be `deny` and not `forbid`: `#[napi]` expands to `unsafe` code wrapped in its own `#[allow(unsafe_code)]`, and `forbid` cannot be overruled, so every `#[napi]` attribute died with E0453 and cascaded into E0425. `deny` still makes any `unsafe` we write a hard error.
- **`emnapi` lives in the root `devDependencies`, not beside `@napi-rs/cli`** — the wasm build has `@napi-rs/cli` require it, and the CLI's realpath is inside `node_modules/.bun/…`, so the only `node_modules` its resolution walk reaches is the repo root's. Declaring it in `packages/tooling` (where the CLI is a devDependency) leaves it unresolvable; it is an *optional* peer there, so nothing installs it automatically.
- **The three emnapi packages are pinned to one exact version, and it must be the version the rest of the tree already forces** — `@napi-rs/cli` refuses to build wasm on a mismatch (`emnapi version mismatch: …`). `@emnapi/core` and `@emnapi/runtime` are pinned exactly to `1.11.2` by `@napi-rs/lzma-wasm32-wasi`, `@napi-rs/tar-wasm32-wasi` and `@oxc-resolver/binding-wasm32-wasi`, so a `^` range on `emnapi` resolves higher and the build dies. Bump all three together, and check the links inside `node_modules/.bun/@napi-rs+cli@*/node_modules/` — the store keeps one directory per peer-set hash, so a stale one can look like the fix did not apply.
- **Clippy pedantic off** — `#[napi]` generates code that trips it; CI runs `-D warnings` instead.

## Open

- The matrix in `native.yml` now reaches the `Build bindings` step on every target: the container jobs were blocked by a missing `unzip` (which `setup-bun` needs) and by Bun having no musl build, and both are fixed. What stopped all of them there was `unsafe_code = "forbid"`, now `deny`. No target has yet produced a binary, so the matrix is still unproven end to end — the `assemble` fan-in and the generated per-platform packages have never run.
- `x86_64-apple-darwin` maps to the `macos-13` runner; a run on it was cancelled manually, so that target's status is unknown. GitHub has been retiring the Intel macOS runners — worth confirming `macos-13` is still available before relying on it.
- Publish ordering across `npm/native` and its generated per-platform packages is out of scope.

# packages/native

The Rust side of the monorepo — a virtual Cargo workspace whose members are crates: **pure Rust crates** that hold the logic, and **binding crates** that expose it to JS via napi-rs, each wrapped by an npm package.

```
packages/native/
├── Cargo.toml            # virtual workspace: resolver 3, members = crates/*
├── rust-toolchain.toml   # stable + rustfmt, clippy, wasm32-wasip1-threads
├── .cargo/config.toml    # build config (WASI linker)
├── .gitignore            # build output, generated loaders, per-platform packages
├── crates/
│   ├── package.json      # @myorg/native-crates — the bridge node (see below)
│   ├── turbo.json        # its Turbo tasks
│   ├── native/           # binding crate — crate-type = ["cdylib"], thin #[napi] wrappers
│   └── shared/           # pure Rust crate — the logic, no napi, plain `cargo test`
└── npm/
    └── native/           # one npm package per binding crate
```

The repo root has **no `Cargo.toml`**. Everything Rust lives here, which is what lets the native config be dropped by deleting one directory.

## How the pieces relate

| Piece | Owns |
| :--- | :--- |
| `crates/<name>/` (pure) | Rust logic — testable with plain `cargo test`, no Node runtime |
| `crates/<name>/` (binding) | Thin `#[napi]` wrappers that delegate to the pure crates |
| `npm/<name>/` | The npm manifest with the napi config, generated loader and types |
| `Cargo.toml` | Members, `edition`/`version`/`license`/`repository`, shared dependencies (incl. `shared = { path = … }`), lints and `[profile.release]` |
| `crates/package.json` | The **bridge node** — the single Turbo package that stands for every pure crate |
| `npm/<name>-<platform>/` | **Generated in CI**, never committed |

## The Turbo graph

Binding packages depend on the bridge package (`@myorg/native-crates: workspace:*`)
whenever their crate has a Cargo path dependency on a pure crate. That mirrors the
Cargo graph into the npm graph, so Turbo orders pure Rust work (`build`, `test`,
`cargo:check`, `cargo:clippy`) before the napi builds that compile it in:

```
@myorg/native ──workspace:*──▶ @myorg/native-crates ──▶ (every pure crate)
        │ napi build                    │ mnative build/test --pure
        ▼                               ▼
   *.node, index.js, index.d.ts    cargo target/ (uncached)
```

- **napi builds are Turbo-cached**: outputs are the stable `*.node` / `index.js` /
  `index.d.ts`, and the `inputs` glob the whole `crates/` tree plus the workspace
  manifests — a Rust change always invalidates the cache.
- **The bridge node is never cached**: cargo owns `target/` and its incremental
  state, and the toolchain participates in cargo's own caching. Its `inputs`
  exist so hash reports reflect Rust changes.

`mnative sync` re-syncs this wiring (bridge node files, the `workspace:*` edges,
the root `workspaces` entry) after Cargo dependencies are hand-edited.

## Commands

All of them go through `mnative`, which discovers crates and packages from disk:

```bash
mnative list              # crates → npm packages, targets per package
mnative add parser        # new binding crate + npm package
mnative add core --pure   # pure-Rust crate, no npm package
mnative sync              # re-sync bridge node + Cargo→npm edges

mnative check             # cargo check --workspace
mnative check --pure      # only the pure crates (what the bridge node runs)
mnative clippy            # clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
mnative fmt:check
mnative test              # cargo test --workspace
mnative napi:build        # build every package's addon
```

- [packages/tooling](../tooling/README.md) — the CLI and the CI matrix that drive this layout
- [npm/native](npm/native/README.md) — the npm package built from the `native` crate
- [Cargo Book — workspaces](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/workspaces.html)

# AGENTS.md — packages/native

> The Cargo workspace. Orientation in [README.md](./README.md), current state in [CONTEXT.md](./CONTEXT.md).

## Rules

- `Cargo.toml` here is the workspace root and must stay virtual — no `[package]` section. The repo root never gets a `Cargo.toml`.
- Never hand-edit `members`. `mnative add <name>` creates the crate, its npm package, and re-syncs and sorts `members`.
- One npm package per binding crate; a pure-Rust crate (`--pure`) gets no npm package of its own — it is represented in the Turbo graph by the bridge node `crates/package.json`.
- Binding crates stay **thin**: `#[napi]` wrappers that delegate to pure crates. Logic lives in pure crates so it is testable without a Node runtime.
- A Cargo path dep from a binding to a pure crate must be mirrored as `@<scope>/native-crates: workspace:*` in the binding's `package.json` — run `mnative sync` after editing Cargo deps instead of hand-editing both sides.
- Never hand-edit `crates/package.json` or `crates/turbo.json` — they are generated (`mnative sync` / `mnative add --pure` / setup rewrite them).
- Every crate declares `[lints] workspace = true` so `unsafe_code = "forbid"` is inherited, and inherits `version`, `edition`, `license` and `repository` from `[workspace.package]` instead of restating them.
- `crate-type = ["cdylib"]` belongs on binding crates only.
- Never commit `target/`, `Cargo.lock`, `npm/*/index.js`, `npm/*/*.node`, `*.wasm` or `npm/*-<platform>/` — all are generated and gitignored.
- Use `mnative` rather than running cargo directly; it applies the workspace paths and keeps one invocation over every crate. The `--pure` flag scopes the cargo commands to the pure crates.
- Never `#![deny(warnings)]` in Rust source — `-D warnings` is a CI flag only.
- Release-profile tuning (`lto`, `codegen-units`, `strip`) lives once in the workspace `[profile.release]` — never in a crate.

## Before marking a task done

- [ ] `mnative fmt:check`
- [ ] `mnative clippy`
- [ ] `mnative check`
- [ ] `mnative test`
- [ ] New crate has `[lints] workspace = true`
- [ ] `mnative sync` leaves nothing to fix (Cargo↔npm edges in place)
- [ ] No generated or build artefacts in the diff

## Architectural decisions

- **ESM-only output** — CJS is not supported. `attw` must run with `--profile esm-only`; node10 and CJS failures are intentional.
- **No `baseUrl`** — TypeScript 7.0 removed it; path aliases use `paths` only.
- **Generated-file system** — every generated file has a source in `packages/tooling/src/`. Never edit output; always regenerate.
- **Zero root devDependencies** — all tools are workspace packages exposing `m`-prefixed bins.
- **Monorepo-wide concerns stay at the root** — git hooks, workflow generation, skills, coverage merge. Per-package work is Turbo's.
- **Native is a virtual Cargo workspace** — `packages/native/crates/*` for Rust, `packages/native/npm/*` for the npm packages; per-platform packages are CI artifacts only.
- **One Pages deployer** — in this repo `template-docs.yml`, so `docs:sync` skips `pages.yml`/`coverage.yml` while `docs/` exists.
- **Coverage gate is 80% lines** — enforced by `mcoverage check` in CI.

# Pixi in a Rust Monorepo — Arena.ai Sandbox Integration Guide

---

## Mental Model

Think of it as **two separate concerns that never mix:**

```
CONCERN 1: The environment          CONCERN 2: Your code
─────────────────────────           ──────────────────────
pixi.toml defines tools             Cargo.toml defines deps
pixi.lock pins exact versions       Cargo.lock pins exact versions
pixi-pack ships the environment     cargo build ships your software
conda-forge provides binaries       crates.io provides libraries
```

The environment is **versioned and released independently** from your code. When you update `rustc`, you cut a new environment release. When you update a crate, you just commit `Cargo.lock`. They never block each other.

The sandbox gets **one tarball** that contains everything it needs to build, lint, and test locally — rust toolchain, actionlint, act, podman. No apt, no brew, no internet inside the sandbox.

---

## Repository Layout

Your monorepo has one `pixi.toml` at the root. It defines feature groups that map to what different roles need:

- **`default`** — rust toolchain only, for building
- **`ci`** — adds actionlint + act + podman, for local CI testing
- **`full`** — everything, for human developers

The workspace `Cargo.toml` and `pixi.toml` sit side by side at root. The `.pixi/` directory is gitignored. The `pixi.lock` is **committed** — it is your reproducibility guarantee, exactly like `Cargo.lock`.

---

## CI Flow (on the internet-connected side)

There are two distinct CI pipelines and it's critical not to conflate them:

```
PIPELINE 1: Pack the environment (runs rarely)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Trigger: pixi.toml or pixi.lock changes
Machine: Standard GitHub Actions runner (has internet)
Steps:   pixi-pack × (environment × platform) matrix
Output:  Release assets on your repo's releases page
Cost:    ~5 minutes, runs maybe once a week

PIPELINE 2: Build and test your code (runs constantly)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Trigger: Every push, every PR
Machine: Arena.ai sandbox (no internet, or restricted)
Steps:   Download env tarball → unpack → cargo build → cargo test
Input:   Release asset URL from Pipeline 1
Cost:    ~90 seconds warm, your code only
```

Pipeline 1 produces the environment. Pipeline 2 consumes it. The agent only ever participates in Pipeline 2.

---

## Download Flow (inside the sandbox)

Three sequential fetches, then fully offline:

```
1. pixi binary          ← github.com/prefix-dev/pixi/releases
                          static musl binary, ~30MB, cached forever

2. environment tarball  ← github.com/your-org/your-repo/releases
                          contains rust + actionlint + act + podman
                          versioned by your release tag, ~400MB

3. (optional) act image ← pre-pulled and embedded or skipped
                          act can run without Docker for lint-only

──────────────── NO MORE NETWORK BELOW THIS LINE ────────────────

unpack → activate → cargo build → actionlint → act
```

The environment tarball URL is the **only thing that changes between sandbox setups**. Everything else — the unpack procedure, the activation, the build commands — is identical across every agent run. This is what the agent prompt encodes.

---

## Two-Stage Bootstrap via Pixi Tasks

There's a subtle but powerful refinement to the download flow: **only the pixi binary needs to be fetched by a raw shell command. Everything after that can be a `pixi task`.**

### The Insight

The environment tarball fetch is itself a scripted operation with inputs (URL, tag, platform, checksum), outputs (extracted directory, activate.sh), and error paths (checksum mismatch, wrong platform). That's exactly what `pixi task` is for. Once you have the `pixi` binary, you have a task runner — even before the environment is unpacked.

This lets you split bootstrap into two stages with different characteristics:

```
STAGE 1: Get pixi         (raw shell, ~5 seconds)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
curl one binary → chmod +x → done.
No dependencies. No task runner needed.
This is the ONLY step the agent memorizes.

STAGE 2: Get environment  (pixi task, ~60 seconds)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
pixi run fetch-env
Reads ENV_TAG from env var or pixi config.
Handles URL construction, download, checksum, unpack, activation prep.
Fully declared in pixi.toml — versioned with the repo.
```

### Why This Matters

**The agent prompt gets simpler.** Instead of encoding curl invocations for the environment tarball, checksum verification, platform detection, and unpack flags, the prompt just says: *"Fetch pixi, then run `pixi run fetch-env`."* All the fetch logic lives in `pixi.toml` where it can be reviewed, versioned, and updated without changing the agent prompt.

**The fetch logic is testable locally.** Any developer with pixi installed can run `pixi run fetch-env` to reproduce exactly what the agent does. No secret sandbox behavior, no drift between "what the docs say" and "what the agent actually runs."

**Platform detection moves out of the prompt.** A `pixi task` runs with a shell and can inspect `uname -m` / `uname -s` to pick the right asset. The agent prompt no longer needs a platform table.

**Checksum enforcement is guaranteed.** The task always runs `sha256sum --check`. There's no path where the agent "forgets" to verify, because the task fails if verification fails.

### Task Definitions

Add these to `pixi.toml`:

```toml
[tasks.fetch-env]
description = "Download and unpack the packed agent environment"
cmd = """
set -euo pipefail

: "${ENV_TAG:?ENV_TAG must be set (e.g. env-2025.07.01)}"
: "${PIXI_ENVIRONMENT:=full}"

REPO="your-org/your-repo"
BASE="https://github.com/${REPO}/releases/download/${ENV_TAG}"

# Platform detection
case "$(uname -s)-$(uname -m)" in
  Linux-x86_64)   PLATFORM="linux-64"      ;;
  Linux-aarch64)  PLATFORM="linux-aarch64" ;;
  Darwin-x86_64)  PLATFORM="osx-64"        ;;
  Darwin-arm64)   PLATFORM="osx-arm64"     ;;
  *) echo "Unsupported platform: $(uname -s)-$(uname -m)"; exit 1 ;;
esac

mkdir -p .tools
cd .tools

echo "→ Fetching env asset for ${PLATFORM} @ ${ENV_TAG}"
curl -fsSL "${BASE}/agent-${PIXI_ENVIRONMENT}-${PLATFORM}.sh" -o env.sh
curl -fsSL "${BASE}/SHA256SUMS"                               -o SHA256SUMS

echo "→ Verifying checksum"
sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS

echo "→ Unpacking"
chmod +x env.sh
./env.sh --output-directory env

echo "✓ Environment ready. Source .tools/env/activate.sh to activate."
"""

[tasks.verify-env]
description = "Sanity-check that all expected tools are on PATH"
cmd = """
set -euo pipefail
for tool in cargo rustc actionlint act podman; do
  if command -v "$tool" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "✓ $tool: $($tool --version 2>&1 | head -1)"
  else
    echo "✗ $tool: MISSING"; exit 1
  fi
done
"""

[tasks.bootstrap]
description = "One-shot: fetch env + verify"
depends-on = ["fetch-env", "verify-env"]
```

### Revised Bootstrap Sequence

The agent's operational script becomes:

```bash
# Stage 1: get pixi (raw shell, unavoidable)
curl -fsSL "${PIXI_URL}" -o pixi && chmod +x pixi

# Stage 2: hand off to pixi tasks (all logic lives in pixi.toml)
export ENV_TAG="env-2025.07.01"
export PIXI_ENVIRONMENT="full"
./pixi run bootstrap

# Activate for the session
source .tools/env/activate.sh
```

Four lines. That's the entire prompt-side bootstrap. Everything else — URL construction, platform detection, checksum verification, unpack, sanity checks — is versioned code in `pixi.toml`.

### When You'd Skip This

If you have exactly one platform, one environment, and no checksum discipline, the two-stage split is overkill and you should just curl-and-unpack inline. But the moment you have two platforms *or* two environment flavors *or* want checksums enforced, the pixi-task approach pays for itself immediately.

---

## How act + podman Fits In

`act` runs your `.github/workflows/` locally by spawning containers. Inside the sandbox:

- **podman** is the container runtime, available in the pixi environment
- **act** is configured to use podman via `DOCKER_HOST`
- The activation script (produced by pixi-unpack) sets up this wiring automatically
- Net result: `act push` inside the sandbox is equivalent to pushing to GitHub

The key insight: because both `act` and `podman` came from conda-forge into the same pixi environment, their paths and library dependencies are already coherent. No manual wiring beyond a config file.

For actionlint you don't need podman at all — it's a pure static binary that parses workflow YAML. Run it before act as a fast pre-check.

---

## Agent Prompt

Give the agent exactly this context block in the system prompt or SETUP_TASK:

```
ENVIRONMENT SETUP
─────────────────
This is an offline sandbox. All tools arrive via a pre-packed pixi environment.

Environment version: {ENV_TAG}           ← operator fills this in
Pixi URL:            {PIXI_URL}          ← operator fills this in

BOOTSTRAP (run exactly once at session start):
  1. curl -fsSL "${PIXI_URL}" -o pixi && chmod +x pixi
  2. export ENV_TAG="{ENV_TAG}"
  3. ./pixi run bootstrap
  4. source .tools/env/activate.sh

The `bootstrap` task handles URL construction, platform detection,
checksum verification, unpack, and tool sanity checks. If it fails,
report the exact output — do NOT attempt to fetch or install manually.

AFTER BOOTSTRAP you have available:
  cargo, rustc, rust-analyzer     — build and check Rust code
  actionlint                      — lint .github/workflows/*.yml
  act                             — run GitHub Actions workflows locally
  podman                          — container runtime for act

WORKFLOW TESTING:
  - Always run actionlint before act
  - act uses podman automatically, no Docker needed
  - Use `act -n` for dry-run if you only want to see the plan

DO NOT:
  - Run apt, brew, cargo install, pip install, or curl to anything
    other than the pixi binary URL given above
  - Assume git, jq, unzip, or brotli are available
  - Attempt to install system packages
  - Bypass `pixi run bootstrap` by fetching the env tarball directly
```

---

## Key Invariants the Agent Must Understand

**One source of truth per concern:**
- Environment version lives in `ENV_TAG`, not in code
- Rust dependency versions live in `Cargo.lock`, not in the environment
- Workflow correctness is validated by actionlint, then act — in that order
- Fetch logic lives in `pixi.toml` tasks, not in the agent prompt

**The environment is immutable from the agent's perspective:**
- If a tool is missing, the fix is a new environment release, not `cargo install` or `apt install`
- The agent should report missing tools as environment gaps, not fix them ad-hoc

**Activation is a session-level operation:**
- Done once at session start
- All subsequent commands inherit the activated environment
- The agent should never re-activate mid-session

**act is a local truth proxy, not ground truth:**
- act + podman approximates GitHub Actions but isn't identical
- Divergence (different runner image, secrets unavailable) is expected and normal
- The agent's job is to get act passing, not to guarantee CI passing

**The pixi binary is the only "raw fetch."**
- Once pixi exists, all further download and setup logic is a task
- This keeps the agent prompt small and the fetch logic in version control


## Manually Dispatchable Bundle Environment CI

### Mental Model

The bundle environment pipeline is **not a reaction to code changes** — it's a deliberate operator decision. You are cutting a new version of the environment, the same way you'd cut a library release. It should require a human to pull the trigger, not fire automatically on every commit to `pixi.toml`.

```
WRONG mental model:   pixi.toml changes → auto-rebuild environment
RIGHT mental model:   operator decides  → rebuild environment → new tag
```

This distinction matters because environment rebuilds are expensive (~5 min × platform matrix), affect every downstream agent session, and should be intentional. A stray whitespace change to `pixi.toml` should not silently ship a new environment to all agents.

---

### Workflow Structure

The workflow has three inputs the operator fills in at dispatch time:

- **`env_tag`** — the release tag to publish under, e.g. `env-2025.07.01`. Distinct from your code release tags. Operators bump this when they want agents to notice.
- **`environment`** — which pixi environment to pack: `default`, `ci`, or `full`. Allows targeted rebuilds without rebuilding everything.
- **`platforms`** — comma-separated list of target platforms. Lets you rebuild only `linux-aarch64` if that's what changed.

The workflow itself does exactly four things in sequence: resolves the lockfile, runs the platform matrix in parallel, publishes assets to a GitHub release under `env_tag`, and posts a summary of what was built and what SHA256 each asset has.

---

### Trigger Philosophy

Three legitimate reasons to manually dispatch:

```
1. You changed pixi.toml          → new package, version bump, new feature group
2. conda-forge upstream changed    → a package got a security patch you want to pull in
3. You're adding a new platform    → linux-aarch64 support, for example
```

One illegitimate reason that will bite you:

```
✗ You dispatch because you're not sure if the current env is good
  → fix this by trusting pixi.lock and the SHA256 summary instead
```

---

### Release Asset Naming Convention

Assets land on your repo's releases page under `env_tag` with names that encode everything the agent needs to select the right one:

```
agent-{environment}-{platform}-{env_tag}.sh

examples:
  agent-full-linux-64-env-2025.07.01.sh
  agent-full-linux-aarch64-env-2025.07.01.sh
  agent-ci-linux-64-env-2025.07.01.sh
```

The agent prompt receives `ENV_TAG` from the operator. The `fetch-env` pixi task constructs the URL deterministically from that tag + its own detected platform. No manifest lookup needed.

---

### Lockfile Discipline

The dispatch workflow should **fail fast if `pixi.lock` is not committed and up to date**. This enforces the invariant that the lock always reflects the manifest. The correct flow is:

```
developer locally:  edit pixi.toml → pixi install (updates lock) → commit both
operator:           sees committed lock → dispatches workflow
CI:                 runs pixi-pack --frozen (never re-solves, uses committed lock)
```

If the workflow re-solved the lockfile itself during CI, you'd get non-reproducible environment builds. The lock is solved once, locally, deliberately, then frozen for all subsequent packing.

---

### Integration with Agent Prompt

The operator updates exactly one line in the agent system prompt after each dispatch:

```
Before:  Environment version: env-2025.06.15
After:   Environment version: env-2025.07.01
```

That single change propagates the new environment to all subsequent agent sessions. Old sessions that already bootstrapped are unaffected — they continue using whatever they unpacked. This is intentional. Environment updates are not hot-patched into running sessions.

---

### Rollback

Because every dispatch produces a tagged GitHub release, rollback is trivial:

```
Something broke in env-2025.07.01?
→ operator changes ENV_TAG back to env-2025.06.15 in agent prompt
→ done, no rebuild needed, old assets still exist on releases page
```

This is the main reason environment release tags must be immutable and never force-pushed over.


```yaml
# .github/workflows/pack-agent-env.yml

name: Pack Agent Environment

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      env_tag:
        description: "Release tag  —  e.g. env-2025.07.01"
        required: true
        type: string
      environment:
        description: "Pixi environment to pack"
        required: true
        type: choice
        default: full
        options:
          - full
          - ci
          - default
      platforms:
        description: "Target platforms (comma-separated)"
        required: true
        default: "linux-64,linux-aarch64"
        type: string

env:
  PIXI_VERSION:      v0.48.0
  PIXI_PACK_VERSION: v0.7.10

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
jobs:

# ── Job 1: Validate lockfile, compute platform matrix ─────────────────────────
  setup:
    name: Validate lockfile + build matrix
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      matrix: ${{ steps.matrix.outputs.value }}

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: prefix-dev/setup-pixi@v0.8.1
        with:
          pixi-version: ${{ env.PIXI_VERSION }}
          frozen: true          # fails immediately if lock is stale

      - name: Assert lockfile is committed and current
        run: pixi install --frozen --environment ${{ inputs.environment }}

      - name: Build platform matrix from input string
        id: matrix
        run: |
          json=$(echo "${{ inputs.platforms }}" \
                 | tr ',' '\n' \
                 | sed 's/^ *//;s/ *$//' \
                 | jq -R . \
                 | jq -sc .)
          echo "value={\"platform\":${json}}" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT


# ── Job 2: Pack one self-extracting .sh per platform (parallel) ───────────────
  pack:
    name: Pack / ${{ matrix.platform }}
    needs: setup
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix: ${{ fromJson(needs.setup.outputs.matrix) }}

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # pixi-pack runs on the CI runner (always linux-64)
      - name: Download pixi-pack (build-host binary)
        run: |
          curl -fsSL \
            "https://github.com/quantco/pixi-pack/releases/download/${{ env.PIXI_PACK_VERSION }}/pixi-pack-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl" \
            -o pixi-pack
          chmod +x pixi-pack

      # pixi-unpack is EMBEDDED inside the .sh for the TARGET platform
      - name: Download pixi-unpack (target-platform binary)
        run: |
          case "${{ matrix.platform }}" in
            linux-64)      TARGET="x86_64-unknown-linux-musl"  ;;
            linux-aarch64) TARGET="aarch64-unknown-linux-musl" ;;
            osx-64)        TARGET="x86_64-apple-darwin"        ;;
            osx-arm64)     TARGET="aarch64-apple-darwin"       ;;
            *)
              echo "Unsupported platform: ${{ matrix.platform }}"
              exit 1
              ;;
          esac
          curl -fsSL \
            "https://github.com/quantco/pixi-pack/releases/download/${{ env.PIXI_PACK_VERSION }}/pixi-unpack-${TARGET}" \
            -o pixi-unpack-target
          chmod +x pixi-unpack-target

      # Also download the pixi binary for the target so agents fetch
      # everything from one release page (your repo, not prefix-dev)
      - name: Download pixi binary (target-platform)
        run: |
          case "${{ matrix.platform }}" in
            linux-64)      TARGET="x86_64-unknown-linux-musl"  ;;
            linux-aarch64) TARGET="aarch64-unknown-linux-musl" ;;
            osx-64)        TARGET="x86_64-apple-darwin"        ;;
            osx-arm64)     TARGET="aarch64-apple-darwin"       ;;
          esac
          curl -fsSL \
            "https://github.com/prefix-dev/pixi/releases/download/${{ env.PIXI_VERSION }}/pixi-${TARGET}" \
            -o "pixi-${{ matrix.platform }}"
          chmod +x "pixi-${{ matrix.platform }}"

      - name: Pack environment → self-extracting .sh
        run: |
          ./pixi-pack pack \
            --manifest-path       pixi.toml \
            --environment         ${{ inputs.environment }} \
            --platform            ${{ matrix.platform }} \
            --create-executable \
            --pixi-unpack-source  ./pixi-unpack-target \
            --output-file         agent-${{ inputs.environment }}-${{ matrix.platform }}.sh

      - name: Compute SHA256 checksums
        run: |
          sha256sum \
            agent-${{ inputs.environment }}-${{ matrix.platform }}.sh \
            pixi-${{ matrix.platform }} \
            > checksums-${{ matrix.platform }}.sha256
          cat checksums-${{ matrix.platform }}.sha256   # visible in log

      - name: Upload artifacts for release job
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: assets-${{ matrix.platform }}
          retention-days: 1
          path: |
            agent-*.sh
            pixi-*
            checksums-*.sha256


# ── Job 3: Create GitHub Release, upload all assets ───────────────────────────
  release:
    name: Publish release ${{ inputs.env_tag }}
    needs: pack
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write

    steps:
      - name: Download all packed artifacts
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          pattern: assets-*
          merge-multiple: true

      - name: Merge checksum files
        run: cat checksums-*.sha256 > SHA256SUMS

      - name: Create GitHub Release
        uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v2
        with:
          tag_name:   ${{ inputs.env_tag }}
          name:       "Agent Environment ${{ inputs.env_tag }}"
          make_latest: false
          body: |
            ## Agent Environment — `${{ inputs.env_tag }}`

            | Field | Value |
            |---|---|
            | **Pixi environment** | `${{ inputs.environment }}` |
            | **Platforms** | `${{ inputs.platforms }}` |
            | **Pixi version** | `${{ env.PIXI_VERSION }}` |
            | **pixi-pack version** | `${{ env.PIXI_PACK_VERSION }}` |
            | **Packed by** | @${{ github.actor }} |
            | **Commit** | ${{ github.sha }} |

            ### Asset naming

            ```
            agent-{environment}-{platform}.sh   ← self-extracting, run directly
            pixi-{platform}                     ← static pixi binary
            SHA256SUMS                          ← checksums for all assets
            ```

            ### Agent prompt update

            Change exactly one line in the agent system prompt:
            ```
            Environment version: ${{ inputs.env_tag }}
            ```

            ### Bootstrap (copy-paste into SETUP_TASK.md)

            ```bash
            # Stage 1: fetch pixi (raw)
            PLATFORM="linux-64"   # or linux-aarch64
            BASE="https://github.com/${{ github.repository }}/releases/download/${{ inputs.env_tag }}"
            curl -fsSL "${BASE}/pixi-${PLATFORM}" -o pixi && chmod +x pixi

            # Stage 2: hand off to pixi tasks
            export ENV_TAG="${{ inputs.env_tag }}"
            export PIXI_ENVIRONMENT="${{ inputs.environment }}"
            ./pixi run bootstrap

            # Activate
            source .tools/env/activate.sh
            ```
          files: |
            agent-*.sh
            pixi-*
            SHA256SUMS


# ── Job 4: Step summary (checksums + prompt snippet) ─────────────────────────
  summary:
    name: Write job summary
    needs: [setup, pack, release]
    if: always()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Download all packed artifacts
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          pattern: assets-*
          merge-multiple: true

      - name: Write summary
        run: |
          {
            echo "## 📦 Agent Environment Pack — \`${{ inputs.env_tag }}\`"
            echo ""
            echo "| | |"
            echo "|---|---|"
            echo "| **Tag** | \`${{ inputs.env_tag }}\` |"
            echo "| **Environment** | \`${{ inputs.environment }}\` |"
            echo "| **Platforms** | \`${{ inputs.platforms }}\` |"
            echo "| **Triggered by** | @${{ github.actor }} |"
            echo "| **Commit** | \`${{ github.sha }}\` |"
            echo ""
            echo "### Assets and checksums"
            echo ""
            echo "| Asset | SHA256 |"
            echo "|---|---|"
            while IFS= read -r line; do
              sha=$(echo "$line" | awk '{print $1}')
              file=$(echo "$line" | awk '{print $2}')
              echo "| \`${file}\` | \`${sha}\` |"
            done < <(cat checksums-*.sha256)
            echo ""
            echo "### Paste into agent system prompt"
            echo '```'
            echo "Environment version: ${{ inputs.env_tag }}"
            echo '```'
            echo ""

            # Emit a clear warning if any upstream job failed
            if [[ "${{ needs.pack.result }}" != "success" || \
                  "${{ needs.release.result }}" != "success" ]]; then
              echo "---"
              echo "> ⚠️ **One or more jobs failed.** Release may be incomplete."
              echo "> Check the pack and release job logs above."
            fi
          } >> $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY
```

---

## What Each Job Does

```
setup    Checks pixi.lock is committed + current.
         Converts the platforms input string into a JSON matrix.
         Fails immediately if lock is stale — before any compute runs.

pack     Runs in parallel, one runner per platform.
         Downloads pixi-pack (build-host, always linux-64).
         Downloads pixi-unpack for the TARGET platform → embeds in .sh.
         Downloads the pixi binary for the TARGET platform → release asset.
         Runs pixi-pack --create-executable → fully self-contained .sh.
         Computes SHA256 for all assets.

release  Merges all per-platform artifacts.
         Creates a GitHub Release under env_tag.
         Uploads: agent-*.sh, pixi-*, SHA256SUMS.
         Body contains the exact bootstrap snippet agents copy-paste.

summary  Writes the job summary table with all checksums.
         Emits the exact one-liner the operator pastes into agent prompts.
         Reports clearly if any job failed, so partial releases are obvious.
```

---

## Three Callouts Worth Noting

**Agents only ever hit your repo's release page.** Both the `pixi` binary and the environment `.sh` are published as your release assets. No agent fetches from `prefix-dev` or `quantco` at runtime — that happens once, on the CI runner, during the pack job.

**`frozen: true` in `setup-pixi` is the lockfile guard.** If a developer edits `pixi.toml` and forgets to run `pixi install` locally before pushing, the setup job fails in under 30 seconds before any expensive matrix work starts. The fix is always the same: run `pixi install` locally, commit the updated `pixi.lock`, repush.

**The agent prompt only mentions `pixi run bootstrap`, not the env URL.** The `fetch-env` task inside `pixi.toml` is the single source of truth for how the environment tarball is located, downloaded, verified, and unpacked. Changing fetch behavior (new mirror, new checksum scheme, new unpack directory) is a `pixi.toml` edit, not a prompt edit. This is what makes the two-stage bootstrap durable.

## Crate Sources as a Separate Release (Cargo Vendor)

### Why Not Inside the Pixi Env

The pixi env carries the **toolchain** (`rustc`, `cargo`, linker). Crate sources are a different concern with a different update cadence:

```
Pixi env:   updates quarterly (new rustc)      → manual dispatch
Vendor tar: updates per Cargo.lock change       → automatic on merge
```

Bundling crates into the pixi env would force a 400MB env rebuild every time a dependency bumps. Keeping them separate preserves the two-pipeline model and lets each tarball evolve independently.

---

### Architecture

Three release artifacts, three independent lifecycles:

```
Artifact              Trigger                  Size      Update frequency
────────────────────  ───────────────────────  ────────  ────────────────
pixi-{platform}       pixi env dispatch        ~30MB     quarterly
agent-env-{tag}.sh    pixi env dispatch        ~400MB    quarterly
vendor-{lockhash}.tar Cargo.lock change        ~50-300MB per dep bump
```

The sandbox bootstrap fetches all three, then goes fully offline.

---

### Vendor CI Pipeline

**Trigger:** Push to `main` where `Cargo.lock` changed. Can be fully automatic — unlike the pixi env dispatch, vendor rebuilds are cheap (~2 min, single platform, no matrix) and idempotent.

**Steps:**
1. Checkout repo
2. `cargo vendor vendor-tmp/`
3. Tar + zstd compress → `vendor-{sha256_of_Cargo.lock}.tar.zst`
4. Publish as GitHub release asset under a rolling `vendor-latest` tag (or a `vendor-{date}` tag)

**Key detail:** The release tag encodes the `Cargo.lock` hash, not a date. This makes it deterministic — two CI runs on the same lock produce the same tag and skip the upload if the asset already exists.

**Naming:** `vendor-{lockhash_short}-{platform}.tar.zst`

---

### Bootstrap Changes

The `fetch-env` pixi task gains a sibling:

```
fetch-env       → downloads + unpacks toolchain tar
fetch-vendor    → downloads + unpacks vendor tar into vendor/
bootstrap       → depends-on: [fetch-env, fetch-vendor, verify-env]
```

`fetch-vendor` reads `VENDOR_TAG` (or derives it from `sha256sum Cargo.lock`), fetches the tar, extracts to `./vendor/`, and verifies the directory is non-empty.

The repo ships a `.cargo/config.toml` pointing at `vendor/`:

```toml
[source.crates-io]
replace-with = "vendored-sources"
[source.vendored-sources]
directory = "vendor"
```

This file is committed. It works identically whether `vendor/` was populated by `cargo vendor` locally or by unpacking the release tar in the sandbox.

---

### Agent Prompt Update

Two new variables, one new bootstrap step:

```
Environment version: {ENV_TAG}
Vendor version:      {VENDOR_TAG}      ← lock hash or date tag
Pixi URL:            {PIXI_URL}

BOOTSTRAP:
  1. curl pixi binary
  2. export ENV_TAG VENDOR_TAG
  3. ./pixi run bootstrap          ← fetches env AND vendor
  4. source .tools/env/activate.sh
  5. cargo build --offline
```

---

### Key Invariants

- **No `vendor/` in git.** The repo stays lean. Vendor sources arrive at bootstrap time from the release tar.
- **`Cargo.lock` hash is the vendor tag.** Deterministic, no human decision needed, auto-derivable.
- **Vendor CI is automatic, pixi env CI is manual.** Different risk profiles — a bad vendor tar breaks one build and rolls forward on next lock change; a bad env tar breaks every agent session.
- **`cargo build --offline` is mandatory in the sandbox.** If it tries to reach crates.io, something is wrong with the vendor tar or `.cargo/config.toml`. Fail loud.
- **Local dev path unchanged.** Developers with internet run `cargo vendor` themselves or just let cargo fetch normally (the source replacement still works if `vendor/` exists locally). The release tar is only for the sandbox.

---

### Rollback

Same model as the pixi env: change `VENDOR_TAG` in the agent prompt to a previous lock hash. Old vendor tars are immutable release assets. No rebuild needed.


# Prebuild Playwright Chromium in GitHub Actions

 If you want to **download a ready-to-use Playwright Chromium build from a GitHub Release**, the basic approach is:

 1. Install Chromium with Playwright.
2. Put the Playwright browser directory into a ZIP.
3. Upload the ZIP as a GitHub Actions artifact and/or Release asset.
4. Users can download the ZIP without running `npx playwright install`.

 Playwright stores downloaded browsers in an OS-specific cache directory, but you can make this predictable by setting `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH`.  Playwright

 ### Example workflow

```
name: Build Playwright Chromium

on:
  push:
    tags:
      - "v*"

permissions:
  contents: write

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v6
        with:
          node-version: lts/*

      - run: npm ci

      # Install only Chromium into a predictable directory
      - name: Install Chromium
        run: npx playwright install chromium
        env:
          PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH: ./pw-browsers

      # Package the browser
      - name: Create archive
        run: |
          tar -czf playwright-chromium-linux-x64.tar.gz pw-browsers

      # Keep it available from the Actions run
      - name: Upload artifact
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v5
        with:
          name: playwright-chromium-linux-x64
          path: playwright-chromium-linux-x64.tar.gz

      # Attach it to the GitHub Release
      - name: Upload Release asset
        run: |
          gh release upload "${GITHUB_REF_NAME}" \
            playwright-chromium-linux-x64.tar.gz
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
```

 Playwright officially supports installing a specific browser with `npx playwright install chromium`; `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH` lets you control where the browser is installed.  Playwright

 ### Downloading it

 After pushing a tag such as:

```
git tag v1.0.0
git push origin v1.0.0
```

 the workflow produces:

```
playwright-chromium-linux-x64.tar.gz
```

 as a **GitHub Release asset**, so users can download it directly from the Release page. GitHub also supports uploading binary files such as `.zip`/`.tar.gz` as release assets.  GitHub Docs

 ### Important distinction

 If the goal is a **public downloadable release**, use a **Release asset**, not only `actions/upload-artifact`.

 - **Artifact** → primarily for files produced by a workflow run; access/retention is tied to GitHub Actions.  GitHub Docs+1
- **Release asset** → attached to a version such as `v1.0.0`, making it suitable for distributing your prebuilt Chromium.

 Also note that this example builds a **Linux Chromium bundle**. For Windows and macOS you generally want separate GitHub Actions jobs/runners and separate archives, because Playwright's browser binaries are OS-specific.  Playwright

      "title": "Git worktree support: reconstitute .git for container mounts · Issue #6074 · nektos/act · GitHub",
      "publish_date": null,
      "excerpts": [
        "Git worktree support: reconstitute .git for container mounts\n* Page: GitHub issue\n* URL: https://github.com/nektos/act/issues/6074\n* State: open\n* Author: jewzaam\n* Created: 2026-04-12T13:51:10Z\n* Updated: 2026-04-12T13:51:10Z\n* Repository: nektos/act\n* Number: #6074\n* Linked PRs: #6075 (open)\nProblem\nWhen act is run from a git worktree, container-based jobs fail because the .git entry is a file (pointer to the main repo's .git/worktrees/<name>/ directory) rather than a self-contained .git/ directory.\nDocker containers cannot follow this pointer back to the host filesystem, causing failures in actions/checkout and any step that needs git metadata.\nAdditionally, when a non-worktree repo contains worktree checkout directories (e.g., .claude/worktrees/ created by Claude Code), docker cp fails because the .git pointer files inside those subdirectories collide during tar extraction with \"file exists\" errors.\nRelates to #657 (closed without resolution).\nProposed Fix\nTwo changes:\n1. Worktree reconstitution (pkg/common/git/worktree.go)\nWhen act detects that .git is a file (worktree indicator), it:\n1. Parses the .git file to find the worktree's gitdir\n2. Reads commondir to locate the main repo's .git/ directory\n3. Creates a temp directory with a copy of the working tree (excluding .git)\n4. Builds a self-contained .git/ directory by copying commondir contents and overlaying worktree-specific files (HEAD, index, etc.)\n5.\nUses this temp directory as the bind mount source for the container\nThe temp directory is cleaned up when the job container closes.\n6. Skip .git entries in subdirectories (pkg/filecollector/file_collector.go)\nThe FileCollector used by CopyDir (which creates the tar archive for docker cp) now skips .git entries (files or directories) at all directory levels, not just the root. These are git-internal metadata and should never be copied into the container.\nThis fixes the case where a parent repo contains worktree checkout directories — their .git pointer files no longer cause docker cp to fail with \"file exists\" errors.\nTesting\n* Unit tests for worktree detection, .git file parsing, commondir resolution, and the copy logic\n* Manual testing with Docker/Podman against repos using git worktree\nEnvironment\n* Tested on Windows (Git Bash + Podman) and designed to work cross-platform\n* Affects both --bind and volume-based (default) workspace modes\n  This issue was created with assistance from Claude Code (Claude Opus 4.6).\nTimeline\n* referenced by jewzaam on 2026-04-12T14:37:11Z\n* cross referenced by jewzaam on 2026-04-12T14:46:21Z"
      ]

/** Extensions that are safe to rewrite as text. */
const SCOPE_TEXT_FILE = /\.(json|ts|js|md|yml|yaml|toml)$/;

/**
 * Repo-relative text files under `searchPaths`.
 *
 * `names` mirrors the filters the discovery passes had inline (`-name "*.md"`
 * for the package docs); omitting it walks every file and keeps the text ones.
 * A missing path is not an error — the pass simply discovers nothing there.
 */
async function findTextFiles(
  root: string,
  searchPaths: readonly string[],
  options: { names?: readonly string[]; exclude?: readonly string[] } = {},
): Promise<string[]> {
  const { names = [], exclude = [] } = options;
  const args = [
    ...searchPaths,
    "-type",
    "f",
    ...names.flatMap((name, i) => [...(i > 0 ? ["-o"] : []), "-name", name]),
    ...exclude.flatMap((path) => ["-not", "-path", path]),
  ];
  // Every discovery pass tolerated a missing path (`.catch(() => "")`).
  const found = await $`find ${args}`.text().catch(() => "");
  return found
    .trim()
    .split("\n")
    .filter(Boolean)
    .map((absolute) => absolute.replace(`${root}/`, ""))
    .filter((relative) => SCOPE_TEXT_FILE.test(relative));
}

/**
 * Every file whose path or contents carry the placeholder scope.
 *
 * Three families are discovered rather than enumerated because their contents
 * grow with the workspace: per-package docs, the per-crate npm packages, the
 * config packages (except the template workspace itself, which is removed
 * later) and the `.agents` tree the skills setup fills in. Duplicates are
 * harmless — both replacements are idempotent — but deduping keeps the write
 * pass to one visit per file.
 */
export async function collectScopeTargets(targetDir: string): Promise<string[]> {
  const targets = new Set<string>(STATIC_SCOPE_TARGETS);

  // Per-package and per-app documentation (README/AGENTS/CONTEXT).
  const docs = await findTextFiles(targetDir, [`${targetDir}/packages`, `${targetDir}/apps`], {
    names: ["*.md"],
    exclude: ["*/node_modules/*", "*/dist/*", "*/target/*", "*/.turbo/*"],
  });
  for (const relativePath of docs) targets.add(relativePath);

# CONTEXT.md

> Snapshot of what is true **right now**. Not rules — those are in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md).
> Not onboarding — that is in [README.md](README.md).
> This file goes stale on the next commit; regenerate it rather than patching it.

Last updated: 2026-09-14

## Repo shape

TypeScript monorepo, Bun workspaces + Turbo.

- `apps/` — one demo HTTP app (private, never published)
- `packages/` — `external` (the only published package), `internal` (private, inlined by Bunup), `native` (optional Rust workspace)
- `packages/tooling/` — the `m` CLI, the scaffolder, and every shared tool config
- `.agents/` — vendored agent skills, one `SKILL.md` per skill
- Generated, never committed as source: `.github/workflows/*`, `turbo.json`, `lefthook.yml`, `packages/native/npm/*-*/`

<!-- TEMPLATE-ONLY:START(template) -->
In template mode this repo is also the template: a scaffolder config that deletes
itself and a docs app (`apps/template-docs`) that the scaffolder removes.
<!-- TEMPLATE-ONLY:END(template) -->

## Packages

| Package | Role | Published |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `@myorg/external` | Public API — the installable artifact | ✅ npm |
| `@myorg/internal` | Shared implementation, inlined into `external` at build time | ❌ |
| `@myorg/native` | Rust bindings built from `crates/native` (opt-in) | ✅ npm |
| `@myorg/example` | Bun.serve demo app, also the Pages artifact (opt-in) | ❌ |

The Cargo workspace root is the **repo root** (`Cargo.toml`, `crates/*`).
`packages/native` holds only the npm packages under `packages/native/npm/`; the
npm package for the default binding is `packages/native/npm/native`. `packages/tooling` is private.

## Configs

27 configs: 17 always-on, 9 opt-in (pruned by the scaffolder when declined), 1 template-only.

- Always-on: badges, biome, bun-config, bunup, changeset, citty, commitlint, community, coverage, dependabot, editorconfig, gitattributes, gh-actions, gitleaks, lefthook, ts, turbo
- Opt-in: codeql (default on), playwright (default on), devcontainer, native, pages, skills, stale, trivy
<!-- TEMPLATE-ONLY:START(template) -->
- Template-only: the scaffolder config (`mdocs`) — self-destructs on scaffold
<!-- TEMPLATE-ONLY:END(template) -->

## Architectural decisions

- **ESM-only output** — CJS is not supported. `attw` must run with `--profile esm-only`; node10 and CJS failures are intentional.
- **No `baseUrl`** — TypeScript 7.0 removed it; path aliases use `paths` only.
- **Generated-file system** — every generated file has a source in `packages/tooling/src/`. Never edit output; always regenerate.
- **Zero root devDependencies** — all tools are workspace packages exposing `m`-prefixed bins.
- **Monorepo-wide concerns stay at the root** — git hooks, workflow generation, skills, coverage merge. Per-package work is Turbo's.
- **Native workspace is at the repo root** — `Cargo.toml`/`Cargo.lock`/`crates/*` at `./`, npm packages under `packages/native/npm/*`; `Cargo.lock` is committed, per-platform packages are CI artifacts only.
- **One Pages deployer** — in this repo `template-docs.yml`, so `docs:sync` skips `pages.yml`/`coverage.yml` while `docs/` exists.
- **Coverage gate is 80% lines** — enforced by `mcoverage check` in CI.

import { existsSync } from "node:fs";
import { homedir } from "node:os";
import { join } from "node:path";
import { resolveConfig } from "@/src/utils/paths";
import {
  defineCommand,
  defineSpawnSubcommand,
  rawArgsAfter,
  runMain,
  spawnTool,
} from "@/src/utils/spawn";
import { skipMissingTool, TOOLS, withOptionalTool } from "@/src/utils/tools";

const ACT_FLAGS = [
  "-P",
  "ubuntu-latest=catthehacker/ubuntu:act-latest",
  "--container-architecture",
  "linux/amd64",
];

const ACTIONLINT_INSTALL = `
'actionlint' is not available.

The 'github-actionlint' package does not bundle the binary — its entry point
downloads a release on first run and caches it under
~/.github-actionlint/bin/<version>/. When that download is blocked (offline,
sandbox, corporate cert interception) the tool is unusable and every run dies
with an opaque TLS error.

Fix one of these:
  bun install --force                                    # retry the download
  brew install actionlint                                # macOS system binary
  go install github.com/rhysd/actionlint/cmd/actionlint@latest
  ACTIONLINT_BIN=/path/to/actionlint m ci:lint           # point at an existing one

Then run: m ci:lint
`;

/** Version the npm wrapper would download, read from its own manifest. */
function actionlintRelease(): string | null {
  try {
    const pkgPath = Bun.fileURLToPath(import.meta.resolve("github-actionlint/package.json"));
    return (Bun.file(pkgPath).json() as { version?: string }).version ?? null;
  } catch {
    return null;
  }
}

/**
 * A usable actionlint, or `null` — decided without touching the network.
 *
 * Resolution order mirrors the npm wrapper's own: an explicit `ACTIONLINT_BIN`
 * first, then a binary already on PATH, then the wrapper's download cache. Only
 * if all three miss is the tool considered absent, because the alternative is
 * letting the wrapper start a download and fail on it.
 *
 * Returning a path lets callers invoke actionlint directly, which also avoids
 * paying for the wrapper's spawn when a system binary is present.
 */
export function actionlintBinary(): string | null {
  const fromEnv = process.env.ACTIONLINT_BIN;
  if (fromEnv && existsSync(fromEnv)) return fromEnv;

  const onPath = Bun.which("actionlint");
  if (onPath) return onPath;

  const cacheRoot =
    process.env.ACTIONLINT_CACHE_DIR ?? join(homedir(), ".github-actionlint", "bin");
  const version = actionlintRelease();
  if (version) {
    const cached = join(
      cacheRoot,
      version,
      process.platform === "win32" ? "actionlint.exe" : "actionlint",
    );
    if (existsSync(cached)) return cached;
  }
  return null;
}

/**
 * Runs actionlint over the workflows.
 *
 * Pass `--if-installed` to skip with a warning (exit 0) when actionlint is
 * unavailable instead of failing. That is what the pre-commit hook uses: a tool
 * that is not installed locally must not block a commit, because CI is the
 * authoritative gate. A plain `m ci:lint` stays strict.
 *
 * Neither mode performs a network operation.
 */
export function runActionlint(args: string[]): number {
  const optional = args.includes("--if-installed");
  const forwarded = args.filter((arg) => arg !== "--if-installed");

  const binary = actionlintBinary();
  if (!binary) {
    // --if-installed is the hook path: skip loudly and keep going, because CI is
    // the authoritative gate. A bare `m ci:lint` is an explicit request to lint,
    // so it still fails — but with the same install guidance rather than the
    // opaque TLS error the npm wrapper used to surface.
    if (optional) return skipMissingTool(TOOLS.actionlint);
    console.error(ACTIONLINT_INSTALL);
    return 1;
  }

  return spawnTool([binary, `-config-file=${resolveConfig("actionlint.yaml")}`, ...forwarded]);
}

/**
 * Runs workflows locally under Docker.
 *
 * A missing `act` is a logged skip rather than a failure, matching every other
 * optional tool here: the developer learns what is absent and how to install it,
 * and nothing that wraps this command — a hook, a package task, a CI job — is
 * blocked by a tool it may not need.
 */
export function runAct(args: string[]): number {
  return withOptionalTool("act", (actPath) => spawnTool([actPath, ...ACT_FLAGS, ...args]));
}

const lintCommand = defineSpawnSubcommand({
  name: "lint",
  description: "Validate workflows via actionlint with shared config",
  argsDescription: "Extra args for actionlint",
  spawn: runActionlint,
});

const actCommand = defineSpawnSubcommand({
  name: "act",
  description: "Run GitHub Actions locally via act with baked-in flags",
  argsDescription: "Extra args for act",
  spawn: runAct,
});

const main = defineCommand({
  meta: {
    name: "ci",
    version: "1.0.0",
    description: "CI tooling for GitHub Actions — lint workflows and run locally with act",
  },
  subCommands: { lint: lintCommand, act: actCommand },
  run() {
    const raw = rawArgsAfter("ci");
    if (raw.length > 0 && raw[0]?.startsWith("-")) {
      runAct(raw);
    } else {
      console.log(`
m ci — CI tooling for GitHub Actions

Usage:
  m ci lint [args]   Validate workflows (actionlint)
  m ci act [args]    Run workflows locally (act)
  m ci:lint          Shorthand for: m ci lint
  m ci:local         Shorthand for: m ci act push

Examples:
  m ci lint
  m ci act -l
  m ci act push -n
  m ci act push
`);
    }
  },
});

if (import.meta.main) {
  runMain(main);
}

export default main;

/**
 * Availability of the external binaries this repo shells out to but does not
 * vendor.
 *
 * One rule, applied everywhere: a missing optional binary is a **skip that says
 * so**, never a silent pass and never a hard failure. Hooks, CI jobs and package
 * tasks all reach for these helpers, so the wording a developer sees is the same
 * whichever entry point tripped over the absent tool.
 *
 * The alternative failure mode is worse than either extreme. A command that
 * exits 0 quietly looks like a pass, so a machine that never had gitleaks
 * installed reports green forever; a command that exits 1 blocks every commit on
 * a tool the developer may not need. Hence: print, then continue.
 */

export interface ToolSpec {
  /** Binary name as resolved on PATH. */
  bin: string;
  /** Human-readable name used in messages. */
  label: string;
  /** What is being skipped, so the warning explains itself. */
  purpose: string;
  /** Install commands, one per platform where they differ. */
  install: string[];
}

/** The optional external tools this repo knows about. */
export const TOOLS = {
  actionlint: {
    bin: "actionlint",
    label: "actionlint",
    purpose: "local GitHub Actions workflow validation",
    install: [
      "brew install actionlint",
      "go install github.com/rhysd/actionlint/cmd/actionlint@latest",
      "bun install --force          # retries the github-actionlint download",
    ],
  },
  act: {
    bin: "act",
    label: "act",
    purpose: "running GitHub Actions workflows locally",
    install: [
      "brew install act",
      "sudo apt install act",
      "go install github.com/nektos/act@latest",
    ],
  },
  gitleaks: {
    bin: "gitleaks",
    label: "gitleaks",
    purpose: "secret scanning",
    install: ["brew install gitleaks", "https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks#installing"],
  },
  trivy: {
    bin: "trivy",
    label: "trivy",
    purpose: "vulnerability scanning",
    install: ["brew install trivy", "https://trivy.dev/latest/getting-started/installation/"],
  },
  cargo: {
    bin: "cargo",
    label: "Rust toolchain (cargo)",
    purpose: "native Rust workspace tasks",
    install: ["rustup — https://rustup.rs"],
  },
  lcov: {
    bin: "lcov",
    label: "lcov",
    purpose: "merging coverage reports",
    install: ["bun run m coverage setup"],
  },
  genhtml: {
    bin: "genhtml",
    label: "genhtml",
    purpose: "rendering the HTML coverage report",
    install: ["bun run m coverage setup"],
  },
  commitlint: {
    bin: "commitlint",
    label: "commitlint",
    purpose: "Conventional Commits validation",
    install: ["bun install          # @commitlint/cli is a workspace devDependency"],
  },
} satisfies Record<string, ToolSpec>;

export type ToolName = keyof typeof TOOLS;

/** The resolved path to a tool's binary, or `null` when it is not installed. */
export function findTool(bin: string): string | null {
  return Bun.which(bin);
}

/** True when the named optional tool is installed. */
export function hasTool(name: ToolName): boolean {
  return findTool(TOOLS[name].bin) !== null;
}

/**
 * Logs an absent tool and returns 0, so the caller skips rather than fails.
 *
 * Always paired with a message naming what was skipped — the point is that the
 * developer can tell a real pass from a skip without reading the source.
 */
export function skipMissingTool(spec: ToolSpec): number {
  console.warn(`⚠️  ${spec.label} not found — skipping ${spec.purpose}.`);
  console.warn("   Install it to enable this step:");
  for (const line of spec.install) console.warn(`     ${line}`);
  console.warn("   Continuing: this step is optional locally and CI installs it.");
  return 0;
}

/**
 * Runs `run` when the tool is present, otherwise reports the skip and returns 0.
 *
 * This is the shape every optional-tool wrapper should take; it keeps the
 * "check, warn, continue" sequence in one place instead of per command.
 */
export function withOptionalTool(name: ToolName, run: (bin: string) => number): number {
  const spec = TOOLS[name];
  const bin = findTool(spec.bin);
  if (!bin) return skipMissingTool(spec);
  return run(bin);
}

 *   mbun       -> m bun             (+ m test)
 *   mbunup     -> m build           (+ m health)
 *   mchangeset -> m changeset       mcodeql    -> m codeql
 *   mcoverage  -> m coverage        mci        -> m ci     (+ m ci:lint, m ci:local)
 *   mgitleaks  -> m gitleaks        msetup     -> m setup
 *   mnative    -> m native          mpages     -> m pages
 *   mskills    -> m skills          mtrivy     -> m trivy
 *   mtsc       -> m typecheck       mturbo     -> m turbo
 *   me2e       -> m e2e

 *

 * command pay only for the module they actually run. The `.then((m) => m.default)`
 * matters — the modules use `export default`, and handing citty the module

  test: () => import("./commands/bun-test").then((m) => m.default),
  coverage: () => import("./commands/coverage").then((m) => m.default),
  changeset: () => import("./commands/changeset").then((m) => m.default),
  commitlint: () => import("./commands/commitlint").then((m) => m.default),
